activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition is often marked with repeat signs, so the performer plays it twice before the development begins.
story:
The deadline was Friday at five, and it was already Tuesday, so Elliot sat at the small upright piano in Ms. Reyes's studio with his manuscript paper in front of him and exactly four bars written down. They were, he thought, the four best bars anyone had ever written, which was possibly the problem, because he was afraid to ruin them with the other twelve.

"Play it again," said Ms. Reyes, who was famous for being taciturn and for drinking tea that smelled like a forest fire. She said everything once and never twice. "Now backwards. Now somewhere in the middle. Tell me what you find."

What he found was that his four bars had a chord change in them that he liked, G to E minor, but that when he tried to extend the melody it kept circling back like a dog chasing its own tail. He had read enough about composition to know that a sixteen-bar melody wanted a shape, an arc, a place to go and a way home. He had also read enough to know that reading was not the same as being able to do it, which was a distinction he found personally insulting.

"It needs a second idea," he said. "But when I put one in, it sounds like a different song crashed into mine."

"Good," said Ms. Reyes. "Two ideas crashing is called music. One idea alone is called a ringtone." She set a deadline with the serenity of someone who had watched a hundred students panic before: the county young composers showcase wanted a notated score by Friday, sixteen bars minimum, chord symbols included, and she had already told them he was entering. "Bring me something honest tomorrow," she said, "even if it's ugly."

That night he lay on his bed with headphones on, listening to a Mozart piano sonata for no reason except that Ms. Reyes had once said, "If you're stuck, eavesdrop on the masters," and he wanted to feel like he was working. His phone buzzed. A text from Dana, who played trumpet and had never voluntarily listened to piano music in her life.

"ok I'm doing the listening assignment," she wrote, "and either the pianist on this recording had a stroke or the file is broken, because he plays like 2 minutes and then STARTS OVER from the exact same place. I've checked twice. It's the same notes. Is this a joke."

Elliot sat up. He pulled up the same recording and counted along. She was right: the pianist played a stretch of music and then began again from the identical spot. He was about to text back "broken file" when he remembered the score reprint Ms. Reyes kept on her shelf, the sonata he'd flipped through once while waiting for his lesson. He found a PDF online and followed it measure by measure. There, at the end of the first section, were two dots stacked vertically like a colon, and back at the beginning, another pair. Repeat signs. In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition was often marked that way, so the performer played it twice before the development began. The pianist hadn't made a mistake. The piece itself asked for the rewind.

"it's not a mistake," he texted. "the exposition is marked with repeat signs, so he plays it twice on purpose." Then, because Dana would not let this go without a fight, he added, "You get to hear the beginning twice and act betrayed both times." Her reply was a single trumpet emoji followed by "i want my 90 seconds back." Somehow this exchange assuaged some anxiety he hadn't known he was carrying: even the masters, apparently, built repetition into their structures on purpose, said "here it is again" and trusted the listener to want it.

He sat back down at the keyboard, but differently now. He had been treating his two ideas as rivals, A material and B material, and trying to pick a winner. What if he let the first idea play, then let the second one crash in, then played the first idea again, changed? It wouldn't be a retreat; it would be a return. He notated eight bars, then borrowed the opening phrase for bars thirteen through sixteen with the chord underneath shifted from G to C, so the same melody landed in a new place, like a familiar street seen from a bus going the other direction. At one in the morning he wrote "DONE (ish)" on the manuscript and fell asleep with his cheek on the piano bench, which his neck would punish him for in the morning.

On Thursday he played all sixteen bars for Ms. Reyes, who listened with her eyes shut in a way that could mean rapture or a nap. When he finished she was quiet for a long moment, long enough for him to consider faking a phone call and fleeing the county.

"The return at bar thirteen," she said finally. "Where the melody comes back over a different chord. What made you think of that?"

"A guy on a recording started over," Elliot said, "and my friend thought he'd had a medical event. So I looked at the score." He told her about the repeat signs, the exposition played twice before the development, and Dana demanding a refund of her time.

Ms. Reyes almost smiled, which on her face was the equivalent of a standing ovation. She wrote one word at the top of his score in red pencil, and he leaned in to read it, and it said: "Again." Then she turned back to the first page and said, "From the top."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Computing a binary search's midpoint as (low + high) / 2 can overflow on very large arrays; writing low + (high - low) / 2 gives the same middle without the overflow.
story:
The room smelled of the radiator and someone's microwaved noodles, and Oliver had claimed the corner terminal because its monitor didn't flicker. He was on his third attempt at the Player class, the one Ms. Reyes wanted stored properly, and this time he had gotten the fields private on the first try.

"No, look," said Dev, leaning over from the next chair. "You wrote the getter wrong."

"I wrote it fine."

"You named it getScore but you're returning name. It compiles. It'll even run. That's the worst part."

Oliver looked at the line. His getter handed back the wrong field, polite and quiet about it, and the compiler had said nothing because both were Strings and both existed. He fixed it, wrote a test in the main method, created a Player, set the score, printed it, and watched the correct number appear. Something loosened in his chest. Encapsulation, Dev called it, keeping the fields locked behind the methods like water behind stone, and Oliver thought of the aquifer under his grandfather's town, the one that had fed every well for a century until the summer the levels dropped and nobody could agree who had drained it. Hidden things stayed healthy until suddenly they didn't.

The competition dataset arrived at four o'clock, a file called round3_large.txt, forty megabytes. Their club had entered the regional algorithm contest mostly as an excuse to order pizza, but they had actually made the final round, and now the search routine had to find player records in the giant sorted array. Oliver had written the binary search himself two weeks ago, and it had passed every test since.

He ran it. The terminal printed one found record, then a second, then a stack of red text he had never seen before.

"That's an overflow," Dev said, pulling his chair over.

"It can't be. The array's not even full."

"Line forty-one." Dev tapped the screen. "You're doing low plus high, then dividing by two. On this thing, low plus high runs right past what an int can hold."

Oliver stared at the line. mid = (low + high) / 2. He remembered the night he wrote it, a Sunday, rain against his window, his mother watching something downstairs with the volume too low to hear. He had been so pleased with himself that evening, the search cutting the array in half and in half again, elegant as folding paper, and he had tested it on the club's sample file of two hundred records and it had worked perfectly. He remembered thinking, briefly, that he was getting good at this. Now forty megabytes of competition data sat in memory and his beautiful line was producing a negative number somewhere deep in the loop where nothing checked for it.

"So it works on the small file because low plus high never gets big enough," Oliver said slowly. "And on this one it does."

"Yes. Write low plus, open paren, high minus low, close paren, divide by two." Dev was already reaching for the keyboard, and Oliver put his hand flat over the trackpad.

"Let me."

He changed the line himself. mid = low + (high - high) / 2, no, he'd mistyped, delete, again. mid = low + (high - low) / 2. Same middle, Dev said, without the overflow. Oliver read it twice. It looked worse than his version, uglier, a workaround dressed as arithmetic, and some small stubborn part of him wanted to argue that his original was cleaner, that the ugliness should count against it. But the red stack trace was still on the screen, impervious to his opinions, and he could not impugn the dataset or the judge or the clock. The code was his. He had written low plus high.

He ran it again. The terminal filled with found records, hundreds of them, then thousands, scrolling faster than he could read, and when it stopped the last line said 2,047,993 matches, 0 errors. Dev exhaled. Priya, who had been watching from the whiteboard with a slice of pizza held like a wand, said, "So we can still submit?"

"We can still submit," Oliver said.

He copied the fixed file onto the flash drive for the upload, and Priya pointed out that they had eleven minutes left, and Dev said the deadline was in eleven minutes or they were dead, it was one of those. At the terminal, Oliver opened his Player class one more time before sending it, hovering over the wrong-getter fix, checking it was really there. He had tested a class today and it had caught his lie. He had tested an algorithm and it had caught his pride.

"Send it," Dev said.

Oliver pressed upload, and the progress bar crawled and crawled across the screen.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aims to make most of it set in form V, the crystal form that gives shine and snap.
story:
The community kitchen on Alder Street smelled of scorched sugar and dish soap, and Madison had claimed the corner station because it was farthest from the door, where the February draft came through like something boreal, straight off a landscape she had never seen. She had with her a dented thermos of coffee, a printout about chocolate, and eleven failed bars wrapped in wax paper. The bars were hers, made in her dorm's shared kitchen over three nights, and every one of them had set dull as sidewalk, bending instead of breaking, blooming with pale gray streaks by morning.

Rosa ran the kitchen's Wednesday night shift and wanted, more than anything she said out loud, a stall at the spring farmers market. She had jars of preserves already, and pepper jelly, and a fussy handwritten sign, but she believed the market wanted something polished, and she had decided that chocolate, properly made chocolate, would underpin the whole table, would give it the finished look the other jars lacked. When Madison unwrapped her failures and lined them up on the steel counter, Rosa picked one up and pressed her thumb into it. It gave, softly, like a candle.

"You melted it too hot," Rosa said, not unkindly, and Madison said she had thought so too, except the printout said the trouble went deeper than heat. She smoothed the page flat between them. Cocoa butter, she read aloud, could crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aimed to make most of it set in form V, the one crystal form that gave shine and snap. Rosa squinted at the page as if it had insulted her in a language she half knew.

"Six forms," Madison said. "And only one of them is the one you want." She had read it four times on the bus and once more in the doorway, and it still seemed to her a strange way for the world to be arranged, that the same substance could set six different ways and only one way counted as right. Rosa, who thought in jars and seasons, said it sounded like honey crystallizing, and Madison said she didn't think it was the same, and then admitted she didn't actually know, and that admission sat between them comfortably, the way shared uncertainty sometimes can.

They worked it out together at the corner station. Rosa hauled out the kitchen's marble slab, cold as a river stone, and a double boiler, and a thermometer with a hairline crack in the glass that made Madison trust it less than she wanted to. She melted the chocolate to a temperature the printout called for, then poured two thirds of it onto the slab and worked it back and forth with a bench scraper, watching it thicken and lose its gloss, then returning it to the bowl to warm gently again. The idea, as she understood it, was a kind of coaxing: seed the good crystals, keep the bad ones from taking over. Her arms ached. The scraper sang against the marble in a thin, high note.

"You're not spreading frosting," Rosa said, watching her. "Less pressure." Madison eased off, and the chocolate moved differently, ribboning off the scraper in sheets that cooled as they fell. She tested it the way the printout suggested, dabbing a smear on the inside of her wrist, and it set in under a minute, dry to the touch. Neither of them said anything for a moment. In the doorway the draft came and went, and somewhere behind them a refrigerator cycled on with a sound like a held breath being released.

She poured into the plastic molds Rosa had brought, tapping out the bubbles, and they waited the full twenty minutes because Madison would not risk rushing it. When she turned the mold over and the bars dropped free, they came out dark and mirrored, and she broke one against the edge of the counter and it snapped, a clean bright report that made a woman stacking dishes across the room look up. Rosa took half the broken bar without asking, chewed it slowly, and said, "That's the stall. That's the whole stall, right there." Madison started to say she'd only done it once, that one success wasn't the same as knowing, that she still couldn't have said why the seed method worked, only that it had, this time, tonight, at this counter.

Rosa was already writing on a napkin, pricing. Madison held the other half of the broken bar up to the fluorescent light and turned it, watching the shine move across the surface like light on a lake that had finally frozen the right way. She put it in her mouth and let it sit. "Six forms," she said. "Maybe next week I get all six." Rosa laughed and said she'd take five, and slid the napkin across the counter for Madison to see.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share.
story:
The classroom above the strip mall smelled of old carpet and burnt coffee, and the radiator had desiccated the air until even the posters on the walls, DRIVING IS A PRIVILEGE NOT A RIGHT, seemed to curl at the corners. Landon sat in the back row with the enrollment form in front of him, reading it more closely than a form probably deserved. Waiver of liability. Terms and conditions. Consent to participate in behind-the-wheel instruction. At the bottom, a line for his signature, and beneath it, a line for a parent or guardian, which his mother had signed that morning in the kitchen, pressing hard enough that the pen had gone through to the counter.

He had never thought about how much of driving school was paperwork before you touched a wheel. You could not simply learn to drive; you had to agree, in writing, to what driving was. The instructor, a dour man named Mr. Reyes who wore his laminated certification badge like a piece of evidence, collected the forms one by one and checked each signature against a roster. When he reached Landon he paused, tapped the guardian line twice, and said, "Tell your mother the ink bled through." Then he moved on.

Under the desk, Landon's phone buzzed. A message from Deshawn: got the lease, read page 6, tell me if I'm crazy. Attached was a photograph of a lease agreement, the apartment on Fairmount where Landon and Deshawn and Priya had planned to live starting in September, if they could sign by Friday at five, because the manager had two other groups asking. Landon had skimmed it once at Deshawn's kitchen table, mostly looking at the rent number, which had seemed fine when divided by three.

Mr. Reyes dimmed the lights and began the first module, right-of-way, but Landon turned his phone sideways under the desk and enlarged the photograph. Page six. He read the paragraph twice. Each tenant shall be jointly and severally liable for the full amount of rent and any damages. He mouthed the words. Jointly he understood. Severally was the one that snagged, and he looked it up on the dictionary app with the brightness turned low, feeling faintly like he was cheating at something.

He read the definition, then the clause, then the definition again, and felt the rent number change shape in his head. It was not divided by three at all. Each of them could be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share. If Deshawn lost his job, or Priya's transfer fell through, the landlord could come to Landon for the whole rent, every month, alone.

"Now," Mr. Reyes said, and the lights came up. "Who can tell me what a waiver actually waives?" Nobody raised a hand. "You signed one this morning. You agreed to it. Did any of you read it?" A boy in the second row said he had read most of it. Mr. Reyes studied him. "Most of it. Interesting. The parts you skipped are the parts that matter to the person who wrote them." He said it without heat, the way someone says something they have said four hundred times, and Landon found himself raising his hand, which he almost never did.

"The liability part," he said. "If something happens in the car, the school's saying we agreed not to hold them responsible for certain things. We consented in advance." Mr. Reyes considered this, then nodded once. "Contracts are just promises with teeth," he said, and moved on to right-of-way at uncontrolled intersections, and Landon wrote nothing for a while because he was thinking about teeth.

He was thinking, specifically, about two pictures of the same idea that did not quite match. His mother signed the school form in one second, trusting the school, trusting him, trusting the general decency of institutions. Mr. Reyes's whole manner, and the paragraph about waivers, suggested the opposite: that institutions prepare for people to fail each other, and that the paper exists because someone, once, did. Which picture was truer? He did not know. Maybe both, depending on the institution, depending on the person. During the break he texted Deshawn and Priya a single question: can we meet at the apartment before five?

They sat on the floor of the empty Fairmount unit because the manager had no chairs yet, the lease between them on the hardwood. Priya had done her own reading on the bus and had the same expression Landon suspected he'd had, the expression of a number rearranging itself. "So if one of us bails," Deshawn said slowly, "the other two could get stuck with everything. Not two-thirds. Everything." Landon said that was how he read it, and that he was not a lawyer, and that they should probably ask somebody who was, except it was four-forty and the manager was tapping her pen at the door.

"We could ask for separate leases," Priya said. "Or a cosigner. Or we could sign it anyway because we trust each other, and that's a nice thing to do, and it's also exactly what the clause is for, people who trusted each other." Deshawn laughed once, without much humor in it. The manager called from the doorway that she needed an answer. Landon looked at the signature lines, three of them, blank and evenly spaced, and picked up the pen, and then set it down again.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, attacked the Marxist social interpretation.
story:
Adam had commandeered the corner table by the periodicals at three-fifteen, before the after-school crowd could claim it, and he spread his notes across it like a general planning a campaign he did not yet understand. The assignment sheet sat at the top: a historiographical essay, two thousand words, tracing how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. He had written the word historiography on a sticky note and stuck it to his laptop, partly as decoration, partly as a threat.

"You're in my spot," said Priya, arriving with a stack of books and an expression that suggested she had been rehearsing the line since second period.

"There are no spots. It's a library. There's just furniture."

"There are spots, and this is mine, and you know it." She set her books down on the far edge of his territory and sat, which was as good as a treaty. She was writing about the Haitian Revolution for the same class, and for weeks they had been conducting a low-grade competition over who could find the more obscure source, a competition neither of them had acknowledged aloud.

His real problem was simpler and worse: the essay required him to identify the moment when historians first seriously challenged the Marxist view of the Revolution, and he did not know when that was. He knew the Marxist view well enough, the bourgeois revolution against a feudal order, the class engine underneath the politics. He knew people had argued against it. He did not know who had fired the first real shot, and without that, his whole structure collapsed into a list of opinions arranged by date, which was the thing Mr. Okonkwo kept warning against. "A list is not an argument," Mr. Okonkwo had said, with the weary patience of a man who had read four hundred lists.

Adam pulled the stack of photocopied journal articles toward him and began skimming for names that recurred. Lefebvre appeared everywhere, Soboul almost as often, both cited as the orthodoxy, the social interpretation, the classic account. Then a footnote in a 1980s article caught his eye: it referred back to "Cobban's celebrated inaugural lecture," and when Adam checked the citation at the bottom of the page, the details assembled themselves like a combination lock giving way. Alfred Cobban, 1954, University College London, delivered as an inaugural lecture and published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution. The article called it an attack on the Marxist social interpretation, and suddenly every later revisionist essay he had skimmed made sense as an echo of that one moment.

He sat back. On the other side of the table, Priya was squinting at a map of Saint-Domingue and mouthing dates to herself. He watched her draw a small frustrated circle around a plantation name, cross it out, and try again.

"That table lamp's flickering on your side," he said. "Want to swap seats?"

"It flickered once. In September." But she gathered her pens and moved around the table anyway, and he noticed she took the article he had just finished, the one he'd set aside, and squared it into her pile without asking. He let her. He understood the code: an exchange of small courtesies licensed an exchange of larger ones.

"Did you know," he said, "that the first serious challenge to the whole Marxist reading was one lecture?"

Priya looked up. "Whose?"

"A guy named Alfred Cobban. 1954, his inaugural lecture at University College London. It got published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution. He attacked the Marxist social interpretation right there, in front of everybody, at his own inaugural."

"Bold way to start a job."

"Right? You get the chair and immediately you torch the field." She laughed, a real one, loud enough that the librarian glanced over with a look that seemed almost atavistic, some ancient ancestral displeasure at noise near books. Priya apologized with a wave.

From where she now sat, closer to the window, Priya watched Adam work differently than he had worked all week. Earlier he had hunched over summaries, hoarding facts. Now he was building, moving articles around the table like pieces, writing in the margin of his outline a line that read, in his cramped hand, "Before Cobban: social explanation dominant. After: questions of politics, culture, contingency." He stopped, crossed out "dominant," and wrote "persuasive," then crossed that out too.

"What's wrong with persuasive?"

"Nothing's wrong with it. It's just doing too much work. Saying one view was persuasive isn't the same as saying it was the only one." He turned the outline so she could see. "That's the thing I keep almost getting. Cobban broke the automatic link between class and event, but that doesn't mean class stopped mattering. It means historians had to argue for it instead of assuming it. So my essay can't be 'Marxists wrong, revisionists right.' It has to be, the ground shifted, and here's what each side saw that the other missed." He tapped the page. "And I still don't know what I think about the Terror. Whether it was inherent in the Revolution or a response to war. I've read four people and they all sound right."

"That's going to be a short conclusion."

"It'll be an honest one." He said it lightly, but he kept the sentence.

The library was emptying. Priya packed her bag, then slid the borrowed article back across the table to him, aligned with his stack, and pointed at his cold coffee. "Bin's behind the biography shelf," she said. He carried the cup over, and when he came back he wrote a new opening line at the top of his outline: In 1954, at University College London, Alfred Cobban stood up to deliver his inaugural lecture and dismantled the ruling interpretation of the French Revolution. He underlined "stood up" twice, then sat down himself and kept writing.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The US Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996 gives food donors limited protection from liability, which encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.
story:
The signup table stood between a folding chair and a dumpster, which struck Eve as either ironic or efficient, depending on how charitable she felt. She had chosen the neighborhood cleanup because the email said food bank volunteers were needed, and because her mother had said the words "college applications" twice in one dinner. She was honest enough with herself to admit that this was the reason she had come. She was honest enough to admit that she didn't know yet whether it would stay the reason.

The basement of the community center smelled of cardboard and disinfectant. A woman named Doris handed her a hairnet and a box cutter and put her to work sorting dented cans, which turned out to have rules: bulging out, throw away; dented seam, throw away; dented side, fine. Two teenage boys, Amadou and his brother, worked the conveyor beside her, and Doris's nephew Dev took photographs for the center's newsletter, an acolyte of good works with a camera around his neck. Eve found herself enjoying the rhythm of it, the small verdicts, each can guilty or innocent of something she could actually see.

Around eleven, a woman came down the stairs carrying four crates of bread, baguettes and focaccia still warm enough that Eve could smell the rosemary. She set them down by the door rather than on the table, like someone delivering evidence rather than a gift. Her apron said SANTOS on it in faded thread.

"Mrs. Santos," Doris said, "you came."

"I came to look. I'm not leaving anything until I understand what happens to me if somebody gets sick." Mrs. Santos folded her arms. "My lawyer friend says one lawsuit and I lose the restaurant. I have three people on payroll. I bake too much on Fridays because people don't show up to pick up their orders, and it's hedonistic, honestly, the waste. But I can't hand out food that ruins me."

Eve expected Doris to argue back, to say something about neighbors or shame. Instead Doris turned to the volunteer sign-in sheet and flipped it over, where someone had photocopied a page from something official and taped it crookedly. Eve was close enough to read it before Doris found the line with her finger. The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996. She read further, over Doris's shoulder, feeling a little like a sneak: the act gives food donors limited protection from liability, which is what encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.

"It's a federal law," Doris said, tapping the page. "Named after a congressman. Limited protection, not unlimited, but it's there so people like you can donate without being afraid."

Mrs. Santos read it herself, twice, mouthing the words. "Limited," she said. "What's the limit?"

"I'm not a lawyer," Doris said, "but it's been enough for Katz's Deli and the pancake place on ninth, and they've been donating for years."

The basement got quiet in the way it does when someone is deciding something expensive. Eve realized she wanted the woman to leave the bread with an intensity that surprised her, wanted it more than she had wanted anything since arriving. She thought about mentioning the rosemary smell, the focaccia, how the volunteers at noon would take it in their lunch break and say her name. She didn't say any of that. It wasn't her bread to be generous with.

"Was it a good lawyer, your friend?" Eve asked.

Mrs. Santos looked at her. "He does divorces."

"Maybe he doesn't do food."

Mrs. Santos laughed, one syllable, and then she stopped laughing and looked at the crates for a long moment. "My mother ran that kitchen before me," she said. "She sent the day-old bread home with her workers in paper bags. Nobody ever sued her, but nobody ever told her it was safe, either. She just did it because it was wrong to throw it out." She bent and picked up a crate and set it on the table, then the second, then the third, then the fourth. She wrote her name on the donation sheet in careful cursive and underlined it.

Doris put Eve on bread duty, bagging rolls in groups of six, and Mrs. Santos stayed to help, telling Eve that focaccia was a Sunday thing, that baguettes sold worse in summer, that Eve's hairnet made her look like a surgeon. Amadou, working faster now that the conveyor held fresh bread, asked Mrs. Santos if she'd bring the same next Friday, and Mrs. Santos said she'd bring more, and then corrected herself: she'd bring the same, because she couldn't promise more, and Doris said the same was plenty.

Eve walked home at one with a bag of rolls she'd been offered and had nearly refused, thinking about the photocopied page taped crookedly to the back of a sign-in sheet, and about the fact that Mrs. Santos's generosity and her caution had both been real, and that the law hadn't made her generous, only made it possible for her to be. Whether that was the same thing Eve couldn't decide, and she carried the question along with the warm bag all the way to her building, up the stairs, and through the door, where her mother looked up from the table and said, "You smell like a bakery."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
story:
The debate tournament shared its building with the theater program, which was how Andrew ended up holding a script in the black box room while sixty debaters argued about jurisprudence two hallways away. He had come to compete, but his partner had the flu, and Ms. Okafor from drama had cornered him near the sign-in table: their student director for the one-act was suspended, the performance was in two weeks, and Andrew, who had done lights for the fall play, was apparently the only person in the building who knew where the board was. He said yes before he had decided to.

The cast was three people: Priya, who talked fast when she was nervous; Marcus, who was calm the way a lake is calm before something drops into it; and a sophomore named Dani who had never performed anywhere. They stood in a loose clump on the stage, scripts rolled in their fists, waiting for him to know what to do. He did not know what to do. He had watched directors work for years and had absorbed nothing except that they said things like "hold that beat" and drank a lot of coffee.

"Okay," he said. "Scene one. Priya, you enter from, uh, the left, and Marcus, you're at the table." Priya walked toward the table from stage right, crossing the whole playing area to get there, and stood behind Marcus's chair looking faintly betrayed. Andrew blinked. He had said left. She had gone right. "No, your left," he started, and then stopped, because she had gone to her own left and that was somehow the wrong direction anyway, and he could feel Marcus watching him work this out in real time.

Marcus set his script down. "Stage left," he said. "That's what it's called." He pointed across the stage. "Stage left and stage right, they're from the actor's point of view, facing the audience. So they're the reverse of what the audience sees." He said it without any edge, the way you'd tell someone which door stuck. Priya crossed to the other side, and this time her entrance worked, and Andrew wrote SL in the margin of his script with a hand that was not quite steady.

He found Ms. Okafor at lunch and told her, half apology and half accusation, that nobody had explained any of it. "Nobody explained debate theory to you either," she said. "You read it, you lost rounds, you figured it out." That was true. His first year he had run a case about obsolete constitutional doctrine, some argument about obsolescent clauses that a senior had handed him, and he had defended it without understanding a word of it until he lost to a girl who simply asked him what the standard was. Losing had taught him more than winning ever did. He went back to the theater with a legal pad and began, for the first time in his life, to write down what he did not know.

The rehearsal that afternoon went badly and then went well. He blocked the whole first scene, drawing boxes on the pad, and when Dani froze in her monologue he almost fed her the line, and then didn't. Instead he called a break, sat on the edge of the stage beside her, and asked what the character wanted. "To be heard," Dani said, so quietly he almost missed it. "Then walk toward him while you say it," Andrew said. "Stage right, two steps." She looked at him to check, and he nodded, and she crossed and delivered the line to Marcus's face, and it was the first true moment of the day. Something in Andrew's chest went hot and clean, the way it did after a round he knew he had won on the merits, though this was better, because it wasn't his.

By evening he had found the two ways of thinking and could not get them apart. Debate had trained him to hold positions he did not hold, to argue a side to its limit and then drop it the second the bell rang. Directing wanted the opposite: a conviction about the scene that he had to keep pressing toward, take after take, without a bell to release him. Yet the arguing had a use here too. When Priya wanted her character to lie and Marcus wanted her to tell the truth, Andrew made them swap sides and defend each other's choice, and out of that argument came a third thing, a compromise that was better than either and that he could not have planned. He still did not know whether he was a person who could commit to one truth long enough to build anything on it. He knew he had blocked eleven pages and the entrance directions were all correct.

At eight o'clock Ms. Okafor looked in from the hallway. "You're missing your own round," she said. Andrew checked the time, and he did feel it, a pull toward the pairing sheets and the fluorescent rooms where he was good at things. But Dani was running her monologue again, unprompted, and Priya had moved a chair without being told.

"I'll take the loss," he said, and turned back to the stage. "From the top. Priya, enter stage left."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A binary search of one million sorted items needs at most 20 comparisons, because halving one million twenty times leaves a single item.
story:
I am not a competitive person, which is why I let Dara talk me into the race in the first place. That's what I told myself on the walk to the coding club, the January dark pressing against the classroom windows when I got there, and it was almost true. Really I wanted to lose. Losing to Dara in front of people would prove something I needed proven: that I was here to learn, not to win, and a person like that could afford to lose.

Mr. Okafor's room still had the antiquated desktops along the back wall, the ones nobody used since the laptops cart arrived, but the club met here anyway because it was the only room with the good whiteboards. I claimed a seat near the middle and opened my laptop on a half-finished file called WordList.java. Dara dropped into the chair beside me and spun a marker like a baton.

"New project," she said. "Dictionary lookup. Whoever finds a target word in the club's word list faster wins. I'll go front to back. You do your weird halving thing."

"It's not weird. It's called binary search." That was the whole of my authority on the subject, a name and a rumor.

"Fine," she said. "I'll do it the normal way."

Theo, who kept the club's data files on a drive shaped like a rubber duck, announced that the list had a million entries, sorted, and he proposed to commandeer the projector so everyone could watch our screens magnified and merciless. A million sounded infinite to me. I imagined the evening ending with Dara somewhere in the C's and me apologizing.

But first, homework review. Mr. Okafor had asked us to build a Java class with private fields and getter methods, and to test it, and I had done this at my kitchen table with a confusion I hadn't admitted to anyone. The confusion was this: why hide the data? If the whole point of a WordEntry class was to hand out its word and its definition, why wrap them in private and make callers go through getWord() like a customs gate? It seemed ceremonial. It seemed like something invented to give tests something to check.

My test file was a small embarrassment. I had written one test that constructed an entry and one that didn't. "That's not testing," Theo said, leaning over, "that's attendance." So I wrote a real one: build an entry, call getWord(), assert it equaled what I'd put in, try to change the field directly and watch the compiler refuse. The refusal was the interesting part. I had expected to resent it and instead felt something closer to relief, the way you feel when a railing turns out to be solid. Dara, whose own class had public fields everywhere, watched my error message scroll up and frowned at it like it had insulted her family.

"Private just means you have to knock," I said, and immediately worried it sounded smug.

"It means extra typing," Dara said, but she opened her file and started changing her fields to private anyway, jaw set, typing getters with the aggression of someone losing an argument she'd started.

Then the race. Theo loaded the million-entry list into both our programs and picked the target: "perspicacity." He wrote it on the whiteboard in his terrible handwriting so we wouldn't claim spelling errors later. Dara started at index zero, her counter ticking on the big screen, one, two, three, a march into a desert. I halved. Take the middle of the list, compare, throw away half the world, take the middle of what's left. The screen made it look casual, my index leaping like a skipped stone, and my counter climbed in a way I didn't believe: single digits, then twelve, then it stopped.

Seventeen.

Dara was at forty thousand and somewhere deep in the B's. She kept going for a while out of dignity, then closed the lid of her laptop, which on the projector looked like a curtain falling.

"Twenty," Theo said, reading off something on his own screen. "Halving a million twenty times leaves a single item. So a search like yours never needs more than twenty comparisons." He said it flatly, the way he said everything, and I sat with the number. At most twenty, out of a million. Dara would have needed, in the worst case, the whole million, or half of it on average, I didn't know which and it didn't matter against twenty.

Here is what I told Dara on the bus afterward, and I want to be honest that I made it sound more finished than it was. I said the class exercise and the race were the same lesson: you accept a constraint, the private field or the sorted list, and the constraint pays you back, order at the door, speed at the counter. I said the railing and the railing's solidity were one thing. Dara listened with her forehead against the window and said, "So hide the data and halve the world. Great slogan. Doesn't tell me what to do when the list isn't sorted."

I opened my mouth and found nothing in it. Because that was the part I hadn't worked out, and the part I'd skipped in my kitchen-table sulk, and the part my neat speech on the bus had papered over. The getters guard the door only if everyone agrees to use the door. Binary search buys its twenty comparisons only if the million entries are already in order, and sorting a million of anything is its own expensive question, one nobody had asked me and I hadn't asked myself. I had been congratulating myself on not being competitive, and then on losing gracefully, and now on winning gracefully, and somewhere in that chain I had stopped checking what I actually knew.

"Theo," I said, texting him from the bus, "how long does it take to sort the list before we can search it?"

Three dots appeared, stopped, appeared again. Dara watched me watch the screen.

"Ask him if the sort's worth it for one search," she said, "or only if you're searching all night."

The dots kept pulsing, and I typed, deleted, typed again, while outside the window the streetlights came on one at a time, in order, all the way down the hill.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
story:
The porch screen at his grandfather's house had a torn corner, and Matthew kept noticing it the way you notice a wrong note in a scale, half listening while he laid his sketchbook pages across the table. Ten drawings, all of them of hands. His grandmother's hands shelling peas, his grandfather's hands on a radio dial, his own hands drawn blind, without looking, in the margins of chemistry homework last spring. The college application wanted a portfolio of ten works around a single theme, plus an artist's statement, and the deadline sat eleven days out like weather on the horizon.

"You've spread yourself all over my table," his grandfather said, setting down two glasses of iced tea. He was a taciturn man who mostly spoke in observations rather than questions, so Matthew answered anyway.

"It's a portfolio. Ten pieces, one theme. I picked hands because everyone in this house has interesting ones." He slid a drawing toward his grandfather, the one of the hands on the radio dial. His grandfather studied it long enough that Matthew began to ruminate on whether he'd chosen badly, whether hands were too obvious, whether the admissions people had seen a hundred portfolios of hands and sighed at every one.

His grandmother came out with her own sketchbook, a fat canvas thing with a rubber band holding it shut. She had gone back to drawing at sixty-eight, taking a class at the community center, and she sat down and opened it to a page of loose clippings. "I've been collecting this," she said. "For my show at the library."

Matthew leaned over. It was a photocopy of a page from some guide for artists, with two paragraphs marked in yellow. "Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement," he read aloud, "a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words."

"That's what my teacher says," his grandmother said. "The short one goes on the little card next to the picture on the wall. The long one goes in the application or the file." She tapped the photocopy. "I wrote my short one first and it was terrible. Two hundred words of nothing. Then I wrote the long one, and when I went back, the short one came out true."

Matthew sat with that. He had been treating the statement as a single hoop to jump through, one paragraph he could polish and send everywhere, and the idea that it might come in two sizes, doing two different jobs, rearranged something in his thinking. The wall card and the application were different rooms. A person standing in front of a drawing read differently than a person sitting at a desk with a stack of folders.

"Can I borrow this?" he asked.

"It's yours. I have the book inside."

He read the marked paragraphs again, then turned to a blank page and started on the long version, because his grandmother had done it in that order and because he suddenly had too much to say for fifty words anyway. He wrote about his grandfather's hands, how they had rebuilt the porch railing two summers ago, how the drawings were partly about work and partly about the fact that hands tell on people, that you can read a life in the knuckles. He wrote about drawing his own hands blind, how the lines went wrong in honest ways. Somewhere in the middle of it he stopped performing for an imaginary admissions officer and started describing what he had actually done, and the difference, though he couldn't have named it, showed up on the page as plainer sentences.

Then he counted backward. He tried to compress the long version and got it to about 140 words, which was still too many, and stared at the torn screen while he thought. His grandfather went in for more ice. His grandmother drew the porch itself, the swing and its shadow, working without comment, and Matthew watched her hand move and understood that she was doing in front of him the very thing his portfolio was about. He cut adjectives. He cut the sentence about honesty, since the drawings were right there to make that argument themselves. He got down to 92 words, counted twice, and read it under his breath.

"Say it out loud," his grandmother said without looking up.

He did. It was six sentences. It said the theme was hands, that hands record work and age and attention, and that ten drawings let him look closely at three pairs of them, his included. It sounded like him, he thought, or close enough.

His grandfather came back out with the ice and sat listening to the screen door bang shut behind him. "Which pair is hardest to draw?" he asked.

"Mine," Matthew said. "I keep wanting to make them better than they are."

His grandfather considered the drawing of his own hands on the radio dial, the knuckles Matthew had shaded heavier than they needed, and pushed the glass of tea closer to his grandson's elbow. "Draw them again, then," he said. "You've got eleven days."

Matthew turned to a clean page, held out his left hand in the slant of afternoon light, and began.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
Connor had two hours before the pharmacy closed and one night before he had to stand in front of a sophomore health class and explain things he was not entirely sure he understood himself. The peer education program had assigned him the unit on consent, contraception and testing, and Mr. Reyes had said, "You'll do fine, you just have to know it cold," which was exactly the problem. He did not know it cold. He knew it the way he knew the bus schedule, well enough to ride it, not well enough to drive.

He stood in aisle four with his phone out, comparing the shelf against his notes. Condoms were locked behind plastic, which meant he had to press a button and wait for someone to come unlock the case, and while he waited he practiced his first line under his breath. Consent is a yes you can give freely, and can take back. The words felt like someone else's coat. He had learned them in a training where the facilitator had tried to inculcate the idea through roleplay, and the roleplay had been awkward in a way that made the idea feel smaller than it was.

"You're the peer ed kid," said a voice behind him. Maya from his civics class was standing there in her work polo, name tag crooked, holding a clipboard. "Reyes sent me an email. You're presenting fourth period tomorrow, and I'm supposed to be your backup if you freeze."

"I'm not going to freeze."

"Okay." She did not look convinced. She glanced at the locked case, then at his notes. "Since you're here, can I ask you something? Off the record. Not as your backup."

A pharmacist came and unlocked the case without a word, and Connor bought a box he did not need, just so he would have something in his hands. In the parking lot Maya sat on the curb and told him, in a flat hurried voice, that she had an appointment at the clinic across town at eight tomorrow morning, before school, and that she had been reading about options all week and the reading only confused her more. "I have to decide there," she said. "They said decide at the appointment or wait a month for the next opening. And my mom works at the school, so waiting means her finding out before I do it."

"What are the options?"

"Pill, shot, implant, IUD thing. The nurse on the phone said something I wrote down." She pulled out her phone and showed him a photo of her own scribbled notes. Under implant and hormonal IUD she had written less than 1 in 100 a year, and next to the pill a number that was much worse, and then a question mark.

Connor looked at the question mark for a long moment. The training binder had a chart, he remembered, and he had skimmed it, but the numbers had slid past him because they were all just numbers. Now, sitting on a curb with someone who had to choose in sixteen hours, he saw what the chart had actually been saying. "Okay," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "The pill fails more not because it's weaker, but because it's a pill. You have to remember it every single day, and people are people. The implant and the hormonal IUD fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on daily use. They just work, sitting there. It's not about the hormone being stronger. It's about not trusting memory."

Maya was writing this down. "So the smart choice is the one I don't have to think about."

"That's not a rule I can give you," Connor said. "That's the thing I keep running into with this whole presentation. I can tell you the numbers, and the numbers are real, I'm not doubting them. But which one is right for you depends on stuff I can't know. Needles. Your period. Whatever else." He rubbed the box of condoms with his thumb. "That's the part that made the training feel dishonest. They wanted me to hand out certainty."

"You could say that part," Maya said. "To the sophomores. The part where you don't know."

The light over the pharmacy door flickered on, that early melancholic blue of autumn evenings, and Maya stood and brushed off her jeans. She said she would text him after the appointment if he wanted to know how it went, and he said he did want that, genuinely, and then asked if she would still be his backup at fourth period. She said yes, but that if he froze she was going to do more than stand there, she was going to talk, and he told her that was the deal anyway.

That night he rewrote his outline on the back of a receipt. Under consent he wrote: it's about volition, a yes that is actually chosen, and you have to say what that means out loud even though it's uncomfortable. Under contraception he drew a crude copy of Maya's question mark. Under testing he wrote the clinic's address and the walk-in hours, because the nurse had given those to Maya too, and Maya had read them aloud to him like they were directions to somewhere ordinary. He practiced the whole thing once in his kitchen, to the refrigerator, and got through it without stopping.

At 7:52 the next morning his phone buzzed. It was a photo of a clinic waiting room, beige chairs and a fish tank, and beneath it Maya had typed: going in, tell the sophomores the truth. Connor put the phone in his pocket, picked up the box of condoms and the receipt and the marker he'd borrowed from his mother's drawer, and walked toward the school with the sun still low behind him and the outline already softening where his thumb had smudged the ink.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid with a wide base and narrow top shows a high birth rate and a young population, pointing to a growing need for schools and teachers.
story:
The flyer had been taped to the gym door since September, curling at one corner: Build a School, Summer in Kestari, two weeks, applications due Friday. Chase stood in front of it with his phone out, taking a picture, when Priya came up behind him with her own reasons for being there.

"You're applying," she said. It wasn't a question. Priya had been saving for the trip since sophomore year, working Saturdays at her uncle's pharmacy, and she'd told anyone who'd listen that her application essay would be about global citizenship. What she hadn't counted on was the new requirement, printed in small type at the bottom of the flyer: applicants had to submit a one-page analysis of why the destination country needed classrooms. No analysis, no interview.

They ended up in the library during lunch, laptops open. The program's information packet linked to two countries, Kestari and a place called Valden, each with a chart labeled population pyramid. Chase had expected something Egyptian, all triangles and mystery. What he got were two bar graphs turned on their sides, age groups stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top, males on the left, females on the right.

"Which one are we supposed to pick?" Priya asked, tapping the screen. Kestari's chart flared outward at the bottom, wide as a church bell, then tapered to almost nothing at the top. Valden's was the opposite, a narrow base widening into a heavy, blocky crown. Chase turned his notebook sideways and sketched both shapes. "Okay," he said slowly, "so Kestari has a ton of people at the bottom. Young people. The bars are widest for the little kids." He counted the age brackets with his pen. "A pyramid with a wide base and a narrow top means a high birth rate and a young population."

"So?"

"So they're going to need schools. Teachers, classrooms, the whole thing. Look at Valden, it's practically upside down. Nobody's having kids, everybody's old." Priya pulled up Valden's government page and found an article about converting a primary school into a residential care facility, and they sat there for a second without saying anything, the implication settling between them: the same shape that made a country build schools could make another country close them.

Chase started drafting his analysis that night, but the drafting went badly. He kept thinking about his grandmother, who had spent last spring convalescing at Riverside after her hip surgery, and how the ward had been full, the hallway lined with wheelchairs, a nurse telling his mother they were short-staffed again. He'd thought of it as bad luck at the time. Now it looked like a pattern you could read off a graph, the way Valden's shape predicted it, and the thought made him uneasy in a way he couldn't quite name, a low-grade malaise that had nothing to do with the essay and everything to do with what his own country's pyramid must look like underneath the numbers.

The next day he found Priya in the chemistry lab before class. "I wrote it," he said, "but I cut the last paragraph." He'd drafted a conclusion arguing that building schools in Kestari was obviously the right priority, more futures, more potential. Reading it back, it sounded like a person who had never met anyone over seventy. His grandmother had spent her convalescence teaching him gin rummy and telling him about the flood of '87; her value wasn't in her future productivity. He had tried to hold both ideas, the graph's arithmetic and that memory, in the same paragraph, and the paragraph had refused.

"So what's your position?" Priya asked, not looking up from her titration. She had her own problem: her essay draft was all feeling and no evidence, and she knew it, and she needed what Chase had figured out about the shapes. He slid his notebook across the bench, the two sketches side by side, Kestari wide at the base and Valden narrow. "Kestari needs the classrooms. That part's clear, the data says so, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't." He paused, watching the burette drip pink into her flask. "But which country needs more, schools or nursing homes, that's a different question than which matters more, and I don't think the graph can answer the second one. I'm going to write that I'm sure about the first part and not sure about the rest."

Priya copied the sketches without asking, which was fair, since he'd shown them to her. "They might not like uncertainty in an application," she said. "They want conviction. Nascent philanthropists, all of them." Chase laughed, and the bell rang, and he gathered his notebook, the drawings still wet where Priya's sleeve had smudged them, Kestari's wide base blurred into Valden's narrow one at the spine of the page.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: William Appleman Williams's 1959 book The Tragedy of American Diplomacy began the revisionist school, arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War.
story:
The museum's French Revolution wing smelled like dust and radiator heat, and Jordan had been standing in front of a diorama of the storming of the Bastille for ten minutes without writing anything. His essay was due Monday. Not a report on the Revolution, his teacher had said, but a historiographical essay: an essay about the historians, about how views of 1789 had shifted since 1800, and why. He had three pages of quotations from Carlyle and Aulard and Simon Schama, and no idea what any of it added up to.

He moved to a glass case holding a small printing press, the label explaining that pamphlets had spread revolutionary ideas faster than the authorities could suppress them. That was the kind of detail his paper was full of, and the kind his teacher kept crossing out. This is about events, not historians, she had written in the margin of his draft, in green ink. He needed perspectives, arguments, revisions. He needed, apparently, to care about who had told the story and what they wanted.

His grandfather had offered to pick him up at four, which gave Jordan two hours. He sat on a bench beneath a portrait of some deputy in a grandiose collar and opened his notebook. The early writers after 1800 had mostly mourned or celebrated, depending on which side their families had been on. Later, Marxists read the Revolution as a bourgeois seizure of power. Later still, revisionists questioned whether anything so tidy had happened at all. He wrote the sentences and they felt like inventory, a warehouse of opinions with no one inside them.

At four his grandfather was early, waiting in the lobby with his coat still buttoned. On the drive home he asked what Jordan had found, and Jordan admitted the problem: every historian seemed certain, and they all disagreed. His grandfather laughed and said that was the point, that he'd written a paper like that himself once, in 1960, his second year of college.

"You wrote about historians?" Jordan asked.

"About the Cold War. There was a book the year before, 1959, William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy. Started the whole revisionist school." His grandfather changed lanes, unhurried. "Williams argued that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War."

Jordan stared at him. "An American blamed the United States?"

"That's what the book said."

"Was he right?"

His grandfather didn't answer for a long moment. "People argued about it for twenty years. Some of them still do."

When they got to the house, Jordan followed him inside, essay forgotten. The book itself was gone, sold in a move decades ago, but his grandfather remembered the fight it started in his seminar, how half the room thought Williams had committed treason against history and the other half thought he'd finally told the truth. Jordan sat at the kitchen table taking notes on a napkin. What struck him was not who was right. It was that Williams had looked at the same documents everyone else had, the same speeches and cables, and seen something different, and that the difference had lasted, had forced every historian after him to say where they stood.

That night he spread his sources across his desk. The Marxists had a framework, the revisionists had a corrective, the early memoirists had their wounds. He began a new draft arguing that each generation's account of the Revolution told him as much about the generation as about the Revolution, and that the honest move was not to pick a winner but to say plainly what each view revealed and concealed. He could see, dimly, where this left him: with an essay that ended in uncertainty. His teacher might call that a failure to conclude. He kept typing anyway.

At one in the morning his cursor sat blinking after the last sentence, which was about how the historiography had no ending, only revisions. He read it twice. Then he opened his phone and texted his grandfather: was there ever a book that settled it? He waited, watching the screen. The reply came as a photo, the napkin from the kitchen table, on which his grandfather had written a single word, underlined twice. Jordan leaned closer to make it out.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Judaism, a day begins at sundown, so a Seder or a Sabbath dinner is held on the evening that starts the holiday, not the evening that ends it.
story:
The argument had been going since Tuesday, and Connor was losing it in his notebook. His aunt's dining room table was buried in photocopies of the Haggadah, a folded calendar from the synagogue, and two slices of pizza going cold, because his cousin Noa insisted that ancient rules earned their authority by surviving, and Connor, who had agreed to debate her at the youth program on Friday, insisted nothing survived on survival alone. The topic was whether the commandments about festival observance still bound people who lived by train schedules and term papers, and the rules of the debate required them to argue from the text itself, no modern commentary allowed, which meant Connor had spent three evenings reading Exodus like a lawyer reading a contract.

The complication arrived when he finally called the synagogue office to confirm the social hall for Friday night. "You booked it for the twenty-third," the secretary said, "but the Seder is the night of the twenty-second." Connor stared at his own handwriting on the reservation form, where he had circled the twenty-third because the calendar on his phone called the twenty-third the first day of the holiday. He thanked her, hung up, and sat very still while the pizza congealed.

"It's my fault," he said to Noa. "I read the date off the phone. It said the holiday starts on the twenty-third, so I booked that evening."

Noa tilted her head at him the way she did when she thought he was being slow on purpose. "The day begins at sundown," she said, and went back to her photocopies. Connor sat there doing the arithmetic in reverse. If a day began at sundown, then the evening that started the festival was the one before the day the phone named, and every plan he had made was off by a night. He thought about apologizing to the secretary, about the folding chairs, about how a person could be careful and still be wrong by exactly the length of one dusk.

He spent the afternoon on the phone. The hall was free on the correct evening, the folding chairs could be moved, the custodian would stay late if Connor brought him coffee, and the rabbi, who had signed off on the debate, said only, "I'm glad you called before printing the flyers," which was somehow worse than a lecture. When Connor finally sat down at the table again, Noa pushed a passage across to him without comment. It was the verse about the festival being kept on a specific evening, and beside it she had written, in her terrible handwriting, one question: starts or ends?

He understood what she was doing. If the text itself anchored the festival to an evening, then the calendar question was not a bureaucratic accident but the very hinge of their debate. A rule that could organize time this way, that could take a day apart and reassemble it starting from darkness, was either a fossil or evidence that the text thought about time more carefully than his phone did. He had planned to argue that such rules were beautiful and finished, museum pieces; now he found himself annotating his own notes with questions he could not answer. He worked until Aunt Ruth turned on the porch light for no reason he could determine, since it was barely five and the sky was the color of weak tea.

Ruth stood in the doorway drying her hands and watched the two of them bent over the table, her nephew's earlobe red the way it got when he was thinking hard, her daughter's pen moving in circles while she read. She had watched Connor all week treat the Haggadah like a chess problem, all cerebral, no skin in it, and she had wondered whether to say something. She had decided not to. Whatever the boy was looking for, being handed it would spoil it. But now he had moved the folding-chair order and the Exodus commentary into one pile, as though they belonged together, and he was muttering about whether the custodian took his coffee with sugar.

"Uncle Marco takes it with sugar," she said. "The custodian plays chess with him. Bring two cups."

"Two cups," Connor repeated, writing it down.

Noa looked up. "You're going to argue my side now, aren't you. I can see it on you."

"I'm going to argue that the text knows what it's doing with time," Connor said, "and that I still don't know if that obligates anybody. Both of those can be true. That's allowed."

"It's sloppy."

"It's honest. There's a difference, and it's not small." He said it with more force than he intended, and Noa, who won most arguments by waiting, actually set her pen down.

Ruth went back to the kitchen and took the brisket out to thaw, because whichever evening it was, they would need it, and she had lived long enough to prognosticate about appetites rather than arguments. Her own view of the old rules had shifted twice in her life, once toward them and once at an angle, and she had stopped believing that probity required picking a side permanently. Through the doorway she heard Noa say, "Fine. New topic for Friday. We debate whether a rule has to bind you to mean anything," and Connor say, "Deal, but I book the hall this time," and the scratch of two pens starting over.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The community center gym smelled of floor wax and old popcorn, and by the second week of January Elijah had learned to arrive twenty minutes early so he could have the far basket to himself. He was the newest player on the Rockets, a rec-league team that practiced on Tuesdays and played Saturdays, and for the first month everything had gone easily. Everyone was polite. Nobody criticized anyone's shot selection. They lost by four, then won by two, and Elijah thought the team was good.

Then Marcus started talking. Marcus, who was nineteen and worked at the hardware store, had played varsity at the high school and believed he should be the captain, though nobody had voted on a captain at all. At the third Tuesday practice he stopped a drill to tell Devon he'd taken the wrong angle on the pick, then told Elijah he passed too much, then told the coach, a wiry man named Reyes who ran the center's after-school program, that the offense had no structure. Two other players argued back. Devon and Marcus didn't speak for the rest of the hour. In the parking lot afterward, Elijah's teammate Sana said, "We were better when we all hated each other quietly."

That night Elijah was supposed to be drafting a persuasive essay for his composition class, the prompt asking him to take a position that could hold two opposing ideas at once. Instead he texted his cousin Deja, who was two years into a psychology degree at the state school. i need something true to say about a team falling apart, he wrote, not a pep talk, an actual idea. She sent back a paragraph that he read twice at his desk while his essay document sat open and blank.

It's a real theory, she wrote. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing. Forming is when everyone is polite and guards their real opinions. Storming is the conflict part, when the politeness breaks and people fight over roles and status. It sounds like your team just entered stage two, which is not the same thing as falling apart. Some groups never get through it. The ones that do start to build norms, shared expectations nobody has to say out loud anymore, and then they perform. I can't promise yours gets through it. That part's on you.

At Thursday's practice Reyes pulled the team into a huddle before drills and said only, "Work it out among yourselves, I'll be in the office," which was unlike him and which nobody liked. Marcus opened his mouth to start again on the offense, and Elijah, who had never once spoken first in a group, spoke first. "We're storming," he said. Everybody looked at him. "It's a thing my cousin told me. A psychologist, Tuckman, said groups go through four stages: forming, storming, norming, performing. Forming is the polite part, which we did. Storming is this." He gestured at the space between Marcus and Devon where the air seemed to have gone thin. "The fighting means we care who does what. It's not the end of the team."

Marcus folded his arms. "So we're supposed to just fight until it stops being a fight?" Elijah admitted he didn't know the mechanism, only the map, and there was a silence in which several people seemed to be deciding whether the map was enough. Devon, unexpectedly, said that Marcus wasn't wrong about the picks, only about the volume. Marcus said Devon wasn't wrong about the angles either, and then, to forestall the argument restarting along its old lines, Marcus said the word nobody expected: "Captain." He looked at Sana. "You actually run this team already. Take the title."

They lost their next game anyway, by eleven, but the loss felt different, more like evidence than like a verdict. Sana started calling sets with her hands, small signals that condensed what had taken Marcus whole speeches to say, and the nascent system wobbled whenever the other team pressed but did not collapse. Elijah's essay, handed in late, argued that a group and an individual could both be works in progress at the same time, and that the honest position was to hold the theory loosely. His teacher wrote in the margin that the argument lacked a strong logos, a clear spine of reasoning, and Elijah accepted the B without appeal.

The last Saturday of the season they played the Lightning, who had beaten them twice. In the fourth quarter, with the Rockets up three, Elijah caught the ball at the top of the key with an open shot, the shot he had taken at that basket alone all those January mornings, the shot that would prove everything. He passed to Devon instead, cutting without the ball, because Devon's angle was better, and Devon laid it in, and the gym got loud. After the buzzer, Reyes came out of the office where he had spent the entire game, looked at the scoreboard, and said, "Wait, you won without me? I was the one doing the storming theory."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: An arbitration clause requires the parties to settle disputes through private arbitration instead of in court, and in the US it is often paired with a waiver of class-action lawsuits.
story:
The enrollment form came in a plastic sleeve with a pen chained to the clipboard, which Stella thought was an odd way to begin a lesson in trust. She was sixteen, third in line at the counter of Ridgeline Driving Academy, and behind her the Tuesday class was already filling plastic chairs. The man at the counter, Mr. Okafor, slid the sleeve toward each student like a dealer. "Read it, sign it, initial page four," he said, and the girl ahead of Stella signed without sitting down.

Stella sat down. The form was dense, and the language had a way of moving just as she reached for it: release, indemnify, assumption of risk. On page four, a paragraph in slightly larger print said that any dispute would be settled through binding arbitration rather than in court, and that by signing she waived participation in any class-action lawsuit. She read it twice. She had seen the word arbitration before, last month, in her father's kitchen, hunched over his laptop scrolling through the endless terms of his new phone app.

That night came back to her clearly. Her father had beckoned her over with two fingers, the screen's glow on his glasses. "Look at this," he had said. "I clicked agree on this app months ago. Apparently I agreed not to sue them in court. If something goes wrong, we go to some private thing instead. And we can't join together with other people who got the same raw deal." He had laughed, a small dry laugh, and said, "They buried it in the conditions where nobody reads." Stella had ascribed her father's amusement to his usual habit of finding catastrophe funny, but she had gone to bed uneasy, the way you do when you learn the floor of a familiar room has a trapdoor somewhere.

Now she looked up at Mr. Okafor. "What does this paragraph mean, exactly?"

"Arbitration clause," he said pleasantly. "Standard."

"I mean, what happens if something goes wrong."

"Then we settle it privately, not in a courtroom." He was already reaching for the next clipboard.

The girl behind her, a compact person in a wrestling hoodie, leaned over Stella's shoulder. "You're actually reading it?"

"Somebody has to."

"It's driving school, not a kidney transplant."

"Same principle," Stella said, and meant it, though she could not have said exactly what the principle was, only that it involved the difference between agreeing and consenting, which her mother insisted was not the same thing at all. Consent, her mother said, required knowing what you were saying yes to. Her mother had said this about doctors, about boyfriends, about a landlord once, standing in the doorway of their old apartment with her arms folded.

The trouble was concrete: Stella wanted the class. Her mother worked the early shift and her father's car sat in the lot all day, and without a license Stella was asking favors every week, small favors that accumulated like interest. And the class was cheap, cheaper than the other school across town, which now seemed less like luck and more like a clue. She thought of her father's screen. She thought of the girl ahead of her who had signed standing up.

She raised her hand again. "If I cross this out and initial it, can I still take the class?"

Mr. Okafor blinked. "Nobody's ever asked."

"But can I?"

He looked at the paragraph, then at her, and something in his face shifted, less irritation than recalibration. "Let me call the owner." He picked up the phone, and while he dialed, the wrestling girl slid into the chair beside Stella and started reading page two aloud in a courtroom voice, "'The student ascribes all risk of somatic injury to their own person,' which I believe is Latin for 'ouch is your problem,'" and Stella laughed despite herself, a bright involuntary sound that felt like the first crack in a frozen lake.

The owner said no to the cross-out, but offered a verbal assurance, which everyone in the room understood was worth the paper it was printed on, which was nothing. Stella sat with the pen hovering. She thought of her mother in the doorway, arms folded. She thought of the car in the lot, keys eventually in her own hand, the specific exhilaration of a first highway on-ramp, the pedal under her foot. She thought: I can sign this and know what I signed, or refuse it and stay home, and neither choice is clean.

She wrote her name, then, underneath, in small careful letters, "signed under protest," and handed the clipboard back. Mr. Okafor looked at the addition, opened his mouth, closed it, and stamped the form.

"First lesson is Saturday," he said. "Eight a.m."

Behind her, the wrestling girl was still on page six, reading slower now.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
