knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current.
story:
Sarah spread the current map across the picnic table and weighted the corners with her father's least favorite bricks, the crumbly ones he kept meaning to throw out. The map had come rolled in a cardboard tube from her cousin Theo, who was doing a semester at sea and had sent it with a note that read, in his terrible handwriting, "You like weather. This is weather's big sister." She didn't like weather, particularly. She liked knowing why things happened, which was different, and which nobody in her family seemed to understand.

Her little brother Wren wandered out with a popsicle and planted himself on the far bench, dripping orange onto the grass. "What's that," he said, in the tone of someone prepared to be unimpressed.

"Ocean currents," Sarah said. "There's a river of warm water that goes up the Atlantic, and it's the reason England isn't frozen like Canada, even though they're at the same latitude. Look, the lines with the arrows."

Wren leaned over the map, popsicle hovering dangerously. "That's it? It's just a map."

"It's not just a map," Sarah said. "It's an argument."

She had actually said that before she was sure it was true. Her geography teacher, Ms. Okoye, had assigned them each a question to answer for the class, and Sarah's was this: explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. It sounded easy until Sarah tried it, at which point she discovered she had two maps that appeared to disagree. The laminated one from school showed the Gulf Stream ending somewhere west of Britain, while Theo's map showed warm water continuing northeast in a branch labeled North Atlantic Current, curling up toward Norway and beyond. One of them, she had concluded grimly, was a liar.

Wren tapped a spot far in the north, past Norway, where the coast made a hook. "Why is this city in a circle? Did you draw that?"

"I didn't draw anything." Sarah leaned in. The city was Murmansk. Beside it, Theo had penciled something, and she had to tilt her head against the sun to read it. WARM ALL YEAR, ICE-FREE PORT, his note said, and then, less helpfully, GOOGLE IT, I'M OUT OF MINUTES.

"That can't be right," Sarah said. "It's above the Arctic Circle. Ports up there freeze in winter. Every port freezes up there."

"Maybe the map's wrong," Wren said, cheerful. "Maybe your cousin's a dissident. Like he disagrees with the map on principle."

"That's not what dissident means. A dissident is somebody who speaks out against a government, not somebody who's rude about arrows." She got her phone out and typed, shielding the screen from the glare. The first three results were about submarine bases, which she skipped, and the fourth said it plainly: Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current. She read it twice, then a third time, mostly to enjoy the sensation of being wrong in an interesting way.

"It's real," she announced. "The ships can get there in January because the warm water keeps going. The school map just stops drawing it too early, like the ocean got bored."

"The ocean can't get bored," Wren said. "It's water."

"Water is extremely boring," Sarah agreed. "That's the whole problem with it."

They sat with that for a minute. Wren worked on his popsicle stick, and Sarah traced the warm line with her finger, from the Gulf of Mexico up past the Carolinas, across the Atlantic, northeast past Britain, up along Norway, all the way to that circled city in the dark latitudes where the sun barely bothered showing up in winter. It mesmerized her, the way a small warm thing could travel so far and still have something left to give. Though she was honest enough with herself to admit she wasn't sure she could say why the water stayed warm that long, and the websites she'd found used words like thermohaline circulation, which she refused to say out loud in case she got it wrong.

That evening she wrote to Theo, because he owed her a reply anyway and because Wren had suggested, with his dour eleven-year-old solemnity, that if she was going to lecture the class she should have her sources in order. Dear Theo, she wrote. Your map won the fight with my school map. Tell your professor the Murmansk fact did all the work. Also Wren thinks you're a dissident now, which you should consider a promotion. Then, because it was Theo, she added: I still don't get why the water doesn't cool off on the way. Nobody explains that part. If the ocean tells you, write back.

She read the letter over, decided it was fine, and left the map on the picnic table overnight, weighted down with the bricks, so the dew would soften the paper into the shape of the table. In the morning Wren came out first and drew a tiny ship with a flag near Murmansk, sailing through water that, on the map, was warm.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal distance a projectile travels equals its constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air.
story:
The physics hall on the second floor smelled like hand sanitizer and old carpet, and Addison had been standing at the capacitor exhibit for eleven minutes. Two brass plates faced each other across a gap the width of her palm, and a laminated card invited visitors to compute the electric field strength at the midpoint between them. Divide the voltage by the separation, the card said, in a tone that reminded her of a substitute teacher pretending the material was fun. What the card did not say was why anyone should care, and Addison had come to the museum that afternoon specifically to decide whether she cared.

She was here because of her brother's tutor, a man named Dr. Pemberton who charged forty dollars an hour and had told her parents that Addison "lacked the temperament for quantitative work." Her mother had repeated the phrase at dinner without irony, as though temperament were a thing you could be diagnosed with, like a peanut allergy. Addison had wanted, with a fierceness that slightly embarrassed her, to walk into her first physics exam in September and desiccate that sentence. Not refute it. Drain it of moisture entirely, so it crumbled.

"Excuse me," said a voice beside her. A boy about her age, lanyard from some robotics camp, was holding a clipboard and squinting at the brass plates. "Are you doing the midpoint problem? Because I got forty, and the card says check your answer against the dial, and the dial says forty, but I don't know if the dial is a measurement or if it's just, like, displaying what you're supposed to get."

Addison looked at the dial. The needle sat at a lazy forty. "If it were a real measurement," she said, "it would jitter. Needles always jitter. That thing hasn't moved since we started talking." She felt a small, unexpected satisfaction in saying it. Maybe the museum was full of charlatan dials, needles pretending to sense the world.

"I'm Marcus," the boy said. "My sister dragged me here and then abandoned me for the butterfly room."

"Addison." She copied her own work onto the corner of his clipboard, since she'd left her notebook in the locker. Half the voltage, divided by half the distance, which came out to the same forty as the full quotient, a coincidence she found elegant until she realized it couldn't possibly be a coincidence. She wrote a question mark next to it and moved on.

Two exhibits down, a demonstrator in a blue polo was resetting a machine that launched a steel marble horizontally off the edge of a table into a sandbox. A strip of tape on the floor marked the table's edge, and a prize basket sat beside a bucket sunk into the sand. "Predict the landing spot," the demonstrator announced, in the cadence of a person who had said it four hundred times. "Closest prediction wins a holographic pencil. Launch speed is on the sign. Time in the air, I'll tell you, because the light gates measure it: half a second."

Marcus went straight for the bucket, pacing out distances by eye, but Addison stood at the table's edge with her hands in her pockets. The marble left the launcher moving sideways, nothing pushed it sideways after that, nothing slowed it down, so the horizontal speed it started with was the horizontal speed it kept, all the way to the sand. The sign said six meters per second. If it traveled sideways at six for the entire time it was airborne, then the horizontal distance was simply that constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air. Six and a half of a half. Three meters. "Get your tape measure out of my bucket," she said, and Marcus stepped back.

She measured three meters from the tape line on the floor, at a right angle to the table's edge, and dropped the museum's wooden marker into the sand. The demonstrator raised an eyebrow at her, either at the marker or at the fact that she had measured from the edge line rather than the launcher, which sat two centimeters back. She moved the marker two centimeters. It seemed judicious.

The demonstrator loaded the marble, counted down with theatrical patience, and released. The marble left the rail, dropped in its smooth sideways-falling curve, and hit the sand with a sound like a small coin, four finger-widths from her marker. "Holographic pencil," the demonstrator said, and dropped it in her palm.

Marcus leaned over the sand, frowning at the marble's crater. "Half a second," he said. "That's all we needed after the time. One multiplication and you had the whole spot." He sounded slightly betrayed, as if the machine owed more difficulty than it had delivered.

"It needed the velocity too," Addison said. "And a right angle." But she was only half attending. She was looking back down the hall toward the brass plates, where a field of forty-something per something existed invisibly between two metal sheets, uniform and patient, and where a question mark sat beside her arithmetic on a borrowed clipboard. The voltage divided by distance gave the same answer as half over half; she didn't yet know whether that meant something or nothing. She turned the pencil over in her fingers and said, "Come on. We're going back to the plates, and this time I want to know why the dial doesn't jitter."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
The article was about a city council proposal to raise the minimum wage, and Hailey had agreed, in a fit of confidence two weeks ago, to argue the opposing side entirely in Spanish for five minutes. Five minutes. In English she could talk for five minutes about almost anything, but Spanish arrived in her mouth in pieces, like furniture that had to be assembled each time before use. She spread the article across the library table and began circling words she could use: aumentar, empleo, salario. Then she hit the sentence "Según el sindicato, el aumento creará doscientos nuevos puestos" and stopped.

Según. She had skipped over that word a dozen times, reading it as filler, the way she skimmed past "like" in casual English. But something about it snagged her now. The sentence said the increase would create two hundred new jobs, and she wanted that claim, badly, because it supported her side. Only the sentence did not quite say it would happen. It said "según el sindicato", which was not quite the same thing at all.

She texted Marisol, whose mother was from Quito and who took the class mostly for an easy A. Hailey typed: does segun just mean "according to"? like according to who?

Marisol's reply came back fast: "yes! según = according to. spanish news writers use it all the time to show a claim comes from a source, not from the reporter. it's like a little flag on the sentence." Hailey read the message twice. A little flag. So the reporter was not promising two hundred jobs; the union was promising them, and the reporter was only holding the claim up, at arm's length, for everyone to see. She wondered how many times she had imputed certainty to articles that were being careful, how many facts she had absorbed that were really just someone's statement, faithfully carried.

The wondering changed her argument. She had planned to say the raise would cost jobs, a clean counterclaim, but now she saw that she could not stand behind a clean counterclaim either. Her other source, an editorial, was itself full of hedges: according to economists, according to a study, according to the chamber of commerce. Everyone was quoting everyone. She drafted a debate position on a napkin, abandoned it, and drafted again: the evidence was contested, the unions said one thing, the economists another, and maybe, she wrote in Spanish, teniendo dudas es razonable. Having doubts is reasonable. Her teacher would probably find that noncommittal, and part of Hailey worried she was right. A debate was supposed to be a fight. Standing in the middle saying "the sources disagree" felt like showing up to a duel and complimenting both pistols.

On Thursday the classroom smelled like the whiteboard marker Mr. Okafor refused to replace. He called her name third. She stood, and the opening she had rehearsed dissolved, and what came out instead was clumsy but hers: "Mi posición es complicada, pero voy a intentar explicarla." The class laughed a little, not unkindly. She laid out the proposal. She quoted the union's claim, and then she said, carefully, "pero la periodista escribe 'según el sindicato'. No es un hecho. Es una declaración." A boy near the window, Danny, who usually slept through these debates, looked up at that. When her five minutes ran out and Mr. Okafor invited a rebuttal, Danny raised his hand and argued, in serviceable Spanish, that doubting everything was its own kind of dodge, that someone had to decide. It was aimed at her and it was a fair hit.

She got the rebuttal slot and stood again, palms damp. She could feel the pull toward pretending certainty, toward grabbing the union's two hundred jobs or the economists' losses and wielding whichever one won the room. Instead she said, "Danny tiene razón que debemos decidir. Pero quiero decidir con los ojos abiertos." We must decide, yes, but with open eyes. The claim was the union's, the losses were the economists', the reporter's job was carrying both, and hers, she said, was choosing among them anyway, knowing they were claims. She finished eleven seconds early and stood there in the silence, unsure whether she had argued or merely described.

Afterward Marisol caught her at the door. "You argued doubts and still took a side. That's harder than either thing alone."

"I don't know if I won," Hailey said.

Mr. Okafor was writing something at his desk, and when he looked up, his pen still hovering over the grade book, he said, "Come look at this rubric line. I'm not sure what to give you for 'position.'"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
Emma had been stringing fairy lights along the fence for twenty minutes when Priya came out with the bowl of chips and said, "Your knot's wrong again."

"Your face is wrong again," Emma said, but she retied it. The whole team was coming at six for the end-of-season party, and she had volunteered the backyard because her mother had said yes without asking any questions, which Emma understood to mean her mother wanted the noise contained somewhere she could see it. It was the last week of August. On Monday the seniors would drive to colleges in three different directions, and the rest of them would go back to school and the team would be reassembled out of whoever showed up, which would not be this team.

She had learned something in AP Psych that she kept turning over. The teacher had flashed a diagram on the board, five boxes instead of the four everyone expected, and Emma had copied it into her notebook without thinking. Later she looked it up on her own, late at night, because the fifth box bothered her. In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen had added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate. The word was "adjourning." She'd said it out loud twice in her room. It sounded like something a court did, or a meeting, formal and tidy, and what she felt about the season ending was not tidy at all.

The team arrived in a clatter of flip-flops and plastic bags, Grace carrying a cake that said STATES in blue icing because the decorator had run out of room. They had lost in the state semifinal, one goal, with four minutes left, and nobody had talked about it for the whole bus ride home except Becca, who kept saying "we had them" in a flat voice until Priya told her to stop.

Emma grilled the burgers because she had appointed herself grill master, a title with no authority attached, a kind of sinecure she had awarded herself in her own backyard. Grace stood beside her with the spatula anyway, supervising, which Emma permitted because Grace was a senior and because Grace's knee was wrapped and she wouldn't play anywhere next year, college club being out of the question, and Emma wanted to give her something to do.

"Five stages," Emma said, flipping a burger. "Did you know that? Most people only know four."

"Four what?"

"Stages of a group. Forming, storming, norming, performing. That's the famous part. But there's a fifth." She watched the grease flare. "In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate."

Grace was quiet long enough that Emma worried she'd said it wrong, made it into a lecture. "Adjourning," Grace said finally, trying the word. "Like adjourn a meeting."

"That's the one."

"So we're in it right now."

"I guess we started it when the semifinal ended." Emma handed her a plate of done burgers. "That's why the bus was so quiet. It wasn't the loss. Or it was, but it was also this."

Grace carried the plate toward the table, then stopped on the grass and turned around. "That's the worst thing I've ever heard," she said, and her voice cracked in the middle of it, and Emma stood at the grill holding the spatula and did not know whether to cross the yard.

Becca called from the table, "What are you two gossiping about," and Emma shouted back "Psychology," and Becca said "Nerd alert," and then Priya started a debate about whether ketchup belonged on hot dogs that absorbed everyone for ten minutes, which Emma understood, later, was deliberate.

They ended up in a circle on the blankets by the fence, the fairy lights making the grass look sedimentary, layer upon layer of shadow, the oldest part of the evening pressed down under the newest. Becca had the cake knife and was conducting. "Best moment of the season," she announced. "I'll go first."

The stories went around. Priya chose the rain game, the one where they'd all been sliding and had won anyway, mud to the shins. Becca chose her goal against Westfield, and everyone booed her vanity, and she bowed. Grace chose a practice: the day in April when nobody could do anything right and Coach made them run, and they'd ended up walking the last lap together in the dark, and nobody had said a word, and it had been, Grace said, somehow the best part.

When it was Emma's turn she had two things in her head, and she could not make them one. The first was the semifinal loss, the four minutes, the ball going past her stick, because she was the goalkeeper and the goal had been hers to stop and she hadn't. The second was the word adjourning, and the idea that the ending was a stage, that it belonged to the sequence, that it was not a failure of the sequence. She had been treating the loss and the ending as the same wound for two weeks. They were not the same wound. She was almost sure they were not the same wound.

"I don't have a best moment," Emma said. "I have the semifinal. That's what I remember most and I don't want to lie about it."

The circle went quiet. Then Priya said, "You saved eleven shots that game."

"She saved eleven shots," Becca agreed, like a witness confirming.

"Eleven," Grace said, and raised her plastic cup, and everyone raised whatever they were holding, and Emma felt the strange doubled thing where you are being kind to and it actually works anyway.

Later, when the seniors had piled into cars and the lights were still on and she was stacking chairs alone, Grace came back through the gate for her forgotten knee brace. She found it on the blanket and stood there holding it.

"Next year's team won't be this," she said.

"I know."

"But it'll be a team. That's the thing I figured out tonight. The stages start over. Forming and all that." Grace hoisted the brace under her arm. "Except I won't be there for it."

"You could come to a game."

"I could come to a game," Grace said, as if testing whether the sentence would hold weight, and then she walked out through the gate and left it swinging, and Emma watched it move, back and forth, smaller and smaller, until it stopped.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Eye-contact norms differ: steady eye contact often signals confidence in North American interviews, while in some East Asian settings prolonged direct gaze at a senior person can seem impolite.
story:
The swings at Miller Park had been Laura's thinking spot since sixth grade, and tonight she had brought the whole problem with her: Priya, a copy of Priya's practice interview on her phone, and forty-eight hours before they had to give each other feedback in front of the rest of the robotics team. The competition's scholarship interviews were on Saturday. Priya's hands were fine, her answers were fine, and she had looked, for the entire twenty minutes, at a point somewhere above the camera lens.

Laura sat on a swing, not swinging, and watched the video again. Priya's grandmother had coached her first, in the living room, with tea. Look down when the interviewer speaks, she had said, glancing away herself to demonstrate; steady staring at an elder is disrespectful, it makes a conversation into an interrogation. Two days later Priya's Aunt Meena, who did hiring at a logistics firm, had said nearly the opposite: hold eye contact, look interested, look confident, because in a North American interview the candidate who keeps looking away reads as nervous or, worse, as having something to hide. Priya had tried to satisfy both and satisfied neither, and now the video existed.

Laura's own problem was narrower and somehow harder. Last year, when Marcus had crashed the robot into the field wall in the final round, she had said only, it's fine, don't worry about it, and Marcus had gone on believing his turning code was fine, and it was not. She had learned that kindness without truth was just delay. But she had also watched their old captain deliver brutal, precise critiques that ionized the team, splitting everyone into factions over whether he was right, a sectarian little war about feedback style that had ended with two people quitting. She did not want to be either person. She wanted to be the third thing, and she did not yet know what it looked like.

Priya arrived at seven, sandals slapping, and dropped onto the swing beside her. "Tell me the truth," she said. "Everyone keeps saying I seemed shy. I'm not shy."

"I know." Laura turned the phone toward her. "Watch this part. When he asks about your design decisions. Your answer's good and then you look at the ceiling."

"That's my grandmother in my head," Priya said. "She drilled it into me. You don't stare at a senior person in our family, not for long. It's rude, like challenging them."

"And your aunt said the opposite?"

"My aunt said, look the interviewer dead in the eye the whole time, that's what confidence looks like here. She interviews people for a living. So which one of them is wrong?"

Laura pushed off the swing slightly, let the chains take her weight. "Neither," she said slowly, working it out as she said it. "They're describing two different places. Your grandmother's rule fits how she grew up; your aunt's rule fits a North American interview room. The problem isn't that one of them lied to you. It's that you tried to obey both at once, and your eyes ended up in the middle of nowhere."

Priya was quiet for a moment. A jogger passed behind them; somewhere near the slide a toddler was being persuaded, at length, that it was time for bed. "So Saturday I do it my aunt's way."

"That's the part I can't decide for you," Laura said. "Because there's more than one interview in your life coming, and more than one kind of room. Maybe the honest answer is: you learn to read the room, and you get to choose." She stopped, aware of how glib it sounded, like a peroration she hadn't earned. "What I can tell you for Saturday specifically is this. Look at the interviewer when you answer. Not a stare-down, not the ceiling. Just, when you finish a sentence, let your eyes land on theirs and stay there a second. Try it on me now."

Priya turned on the swing, chains twisting. "Hi, I'm Priya Nair, and the lifting mechanism was my subsystem." Her gaze held Laura's, wobbled once, and held again.

"Right there," Laura said. "That wobble. That's the whole note. Everything else in your interview is already good, I mean it, your answer about the torque tradeoff was better than anything I could do. The one thing to change is the eyes, and now you know exactly what to change." She heard how specific it was, how it named the thing instead of the person, and felt something settle that she couldn't have articulated: this was the third thing, or near it, and it had only taken saying it out loud to find out.

"On Monday," Priya said, "when we do Marcus's code review, you're talking first."

"Deal," said Laura, and jumped off the swing while it was still moving, just to feel the ground take her.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Georges Lefebvre's 1939 book, translated as The Coming of the French Revolution, described 1789 as four revolutions: aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular and peasant.
story:
The fan in Grandpa's study made a sound like a slow shovel through gravel, and Victor had been listening to it for an hour without writing anything except his name. The assignment sheet lay beside the laptop: a historiographical essay, due in eleven days, on how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. He had checked out four books from the library and carried them here because his parents' house was loud and this one was not, and because Grandpa never asked what he was working on, which Victor had come to regard as a form of respect.

He had written one paragraph three times. The problem was that historians did not simply disagree about whether the Revolution was good or bad; they disagreed about what it even was, and he could not find a shape that held the disagreement without flattening it. He tried organizing by decade, then by country, then by whether the historian had liked Napoleon, and each time the paragraph collapsed into a list. His teacher's comment on his last essay still sat in his memory, "structure is not a box you impose but a claim you make," which had sounded wise in October and useless now.

Grandpa came through with two glasses of iced tea and set one on the desk, coasters being a religion in this house. "Still the Revolution," he said, nodding at the screen.

"Still the Revolution," Victor said. He typed a sentence and deleted it. "I can't figure out what to do with all of them. Every book treats it like one thing that happened, and then argues about it. But they're not even arguing about the same thing."

Grandpa drank his tea and did not answer, which was his way of not answering. He went back to the kitchen, and Victor heard the radio come on low, the station that played jazz from before he was born.

He got up to look at the bookshelves, partly to move and partly because Grandpa had a wall of old paperbacks he'd bought in used bookstores his whole life, and some of them were history. Victor had always liked the spines, faded orange and grey, the old prices penciled inside the covers, sixty cents, seventy-five. He pulled out a thin one with a cracked spine, thinking it might be a novel. It wasn't. The title page said The Coming of the French Revolution, Georges Lefebvre, and inside the front cover his grandfather's handwriting, small and ascetic, gave a date from before either of Victor's parents was born. 1939, said the copyright page, and Victor remembered seeing the name in one of his library books, mentioned in passing and then passed over.

He read standing up, one hip against the shelf, the fan going behind him. Lefebvre laid it out plainly: 1789 was not one revolution but four, an aristocratic revolution, a bourgeois revolution, an urban popular revolution, and a peasant revolution, all unfolding at once. Victor read the page twice. The historians he'd been trying to stack into a single argument were not describing the same object at all. Some of them had been arguing about the bourgeois one, others about the peasant one, and the books that called the whole thing a catastrophe were often really talking about the urban streets, the crowds, the violence, while the books that called it a beginning were talking about laws and assemblies. It was not that they disagreed. It was that the Revolution itself was plural, and every historian held up one of its faces to the light.

He sat back down and wrote a new first paragraph, borrowing the four revolutions as scaffolding, and for the first time the sentences came out in an order he believed. Then he stopped, because a worry arrived. If he used Lefebvre's structure, was he deciding the question his essay was supposed to be asking? Lefebvre in 1939 was one view among many, a man writing between two wars with his own commitments, and later historians had pushed back against exactly this story of a bourgeois revolution taking center stage. Victor sat with that. He was not sure the borrowing was neutral, and he was not sure it was dishonest either. Maybe a structure could be a hypothesis. He wrote a sentence acknowledging that Lefebvre's fourfold account was itself part of the history of opinions, not outside it, then deleted "history of opinions" as clumsy and put "the argument itself" instead.

He carried the book to the kitchen. "Did you read this when you bought it?"

Grandpa turned the radio down. He looked at the cover for a moment, the way people look at something they had forgotten they owned, and Victor understood that the book had been sitting on that shelf through every summer of his childhood, seismic in his essay tonight and inert for forty years before that.

"I read it on a bus," Grandpa said. "Coming back from a job I quit. I was deciding what to do with myself." He set the book on the counter between them, spine up, and turned the radio off entirely. "What did you find in it?"

"A way to parametrize the whole mess," Victor said. "Four revolutions instead of one. I think I can build the essay on it, if I'm honest about where it breaks."

Grandpa nodded slowly, and pushed the book back across the counter toward him.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
The clinic smelled like the inside of a binder, all paper and antiseptic, and Victor sat on the crinkling exam table with his sleeve rolled up, trying to look like someone who belonged in a body that was being inspected. He was here for his college physical, but also, according to the packet in his backpack, for something else: in September he would start training as a peer health educator, and before the first session he was supposed to be able to explain consent, contraception, and where a person could get tested for infections. His own doctor, Dr. Okafor, had agreed to let him practice on her, which was either a kindness or a trap.

The blood pressure cuff tightened around his arm like it had opinions. Dr. Okafor watched the numbers and frowned, just slightly, the way you frown at a typo in someone else's essay.

"That's high," she said. "Were you nervous coming in?"

"A little," Victor admitted. "Also my mom has hypertension. Congenital stuff runs in my family, or maybe it doesn't, I don't actually know what counts as inherited and what's just... habits."

She wrote something down. "Do you know what your pressure reads at home?"

"We don't have a cuff."

Dr. Okafor nodded and unwound the cuff from his arm. "There's a thing called white coat hypertension," she said. "Pressure reads high here in the clinic, often from nervousness, but it's normal at home. So before I conclude anything, I'd want to check it with home readings, or a monitor you wear all day. One number, one time, in one room, doesn't tell the story."

Victor looked at his own arm, at the pink crease the cuff had left. He had walked in here certain that one reading would instantiate his fate, that the machine would look into him and hand him his heredity like a sealed envelope. The idea that the building itself could be a variable, that the same body could say different things in different rooms, was strange and a little relieving. "So how would I get the monitor?" he asked, and she wrote him a referral and told him the pharmacy kept loaners, and he folded the paper into his packet, where it sat on top of the health educator checklist.

"That's what you wanted to practice?" she said, tapping the packet. "Go ahead. Pretend I'm seventeen and clueless."

He stumbled at first. Consent, he said, was about permission that could be taken back, that had to be clear and ongoing, not assumed from silence or from what happened yesterday. He made her repeat it back to him, which felt absurd with a woman who had checked his tonsils since he was four, but she played along, and the repetition was the point: he was supposed to make the other person say it, not just nod. With contraception he did better, laying out the options like islands in an archipelago, condoms and pills and IUDs, each with its own failure rates and its own logic, no single one the whole answer. She asked questions a real seventeen-year-old might ask, whether two methods were better than one, whether you could feel an IUD, and he answered, and where he didn't know he said so.

The testing part was where his voice thinned. He explained that the campus clinic did it, that it was often free or cheap, that results were confidential even from parents, that you could ask for a full panel and not just what they offered by default. He heard himself say the words and realized he had never said any of them out loud before, only read them in the training modules at midnight with his door shut, and that some part of him had planned to keep that silence going even while standing in front of a classroom teaching other people to break it.

"Better," Dr. Okafor said. "You'll get smoother. You should also know you're going to get it wrong sometimes, say something clumsy, have a kid laugh at you. That's the job."

"Great," Victor said. "The job sounds terrible."

"The job is the reason a kid who's too embarrassed to ask me might ask you." She looked at the referral slip, then at his arm again, and said that in the meantime he should take his own pressure at the drugstore machine, twice, on days he felt calm, and bring her the numbers. Not to decide anything yet. Just to see what his body said when nobody in a white coat was in the room.

In the parking lot he called his mom to say the physical was fine, mostly, probably, pending. He sat on the curb afterward with the packet open on his knees, the referral slip beside the checklist, and texted the friend who had dared him to apply for the training in the first place: guess I have to practice on you next. He pressed send before he could reread it, and watched the three dots appear.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index.
story:
Gabriella had promised herself she would finish the essay before Sunday, but by Friday afternoon the document on her laptop was still two paragraphs long, and the second paragraph was mostly a sentence she had deleted three times and retyped twice. The assignment asked her to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation, and to do it in plain language, as if to someone with no training. She had come to her grandmother's house for the weekend because the apartment she shared with two roommates had turned into a place where nothing got written, and because her grandmother, who had run a hardware store for thirty-one years, was the plainest speaker she knew.

She found her grandmother on the back porch shellading a chair, brush moving in long strokes, the smell of varnish warm in the September air. Gabriella set the laptop on the rail and said she needed a favor. She needed to explain something out loud, to a person, and she needed that person to interrupt whenever the explanation stopped making sense.

Her grandmother dipped the brush and said, "Go ahead, then. I'm listening."

Gabriella began the way the textbook began, which was a mistake. She talked about the money supply, then about aggregate demand, then about the transmission mechanism, and within four minutes her grandmother had set the brush down and was looking at her with the expression she reserved for a customer who couldn't decide between two kinds of paint. "You've just said a lot of words in a row," her grandmother said. "I counted. I stopped counting at forty." Gabriella scrolled back through her draft and saw that her second paragraph was prolix in exactly the way her teacher had warned against, dense and formal and hiding the fact that she didn't actually understand the chain of reasoning herself.

So she tried a different approach, the way her grandmother would have run it in the store. Suppose, she said, borrowing is very cheap. You'd take out a loan for the delivery van you've been wanting, and so would everyone else, and all that buying pushes prices up, because there's more money chasing the same shelves of goods. Now suppose the central bank raises interest rates. The loan for the van costs more every month, so you wait. So does everyone else. Less buying, cooler prices. Her grandmother picked the brush back up. "That I understand," she said. "That's just the cost of money." But then she asked the question Gabriella had been circling all week: cooled to what? What was the number the bank was aiming at?

Gabriella opened her laptop and searched, and there it was, in a Federal Reserve press release she'd skimmed past a dozen times. On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index. Not the grocery-bill number people talked about at parties, but the PCE index, a broader measure. She read the line aloud twice. She had assumed the 2 percent figure was some kind of natural law, ancient and settled, and discovering that it had been made explicit on a specific January day, in her own lifetime, changed the shape of the whole essay. A target was a choice. Someone had sat in a room and decided that a little inflation was healthier than none, and had written that decision down so the public could hold them to it.

She tested the explanation again, standing at the rail while her grandmother sanded a run in the varnish. Raise rates, borrowing slows, spending slows, price pressure eases, and you ease it toward 2 percent, not toward zero, because zero leaves no cushion. Her grandmother asked whether raising rates could go too far, whether you could cauterize the wound so thoroughly you killed the patient, and Gabriella laughed and said that was exactly the critique she wanted in her third paragraph, though she'd phrase it less vividly. She liked that the analogy worked both ways: the tool was real, and it could burn.

That evening she typed until the kitchen light behind her went from gold to gray. There was an exhilaration in it that she hadn't expected, the feeling of an argument snapping into place, each link able to hold a person's weight. She wrote the plain version first, the van and the shelves, and put the machinery underneath it. She kept the questions her grandmother had asked in the margins of her mind, especially the one about how long the cooling takes, how a family waiting to buy a house experiences a year of higher rates as neither abstract nor temporary. Her essay would have to say that the mechanism was understood and the timing was not, and she found she preferred that honesty to a tidier conclusion. She saved the file, then saved it again to a second place, the way her grandmother kept a cash box under the register no matter what the bank said.

Her grandmother came out with two cups of tea and set one beside the laptop. She looked over Gabriella's shoulder at the last line on the screen, then out at the yard, where the evening had gone blue and the shellacked chair was drying in rows of pale light.

"Two percent," her grandmother said. "Written down, for everyone to see. I like that they signed their name to it."

"I'll take that as my epigraph," Gabriella said, and pulled the laptop closer.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Slowing inflation by raising rates usually costs jobs: during the US recession of the early 1980s, unemployment rose above 10 percent.
story:
Mr. Okafor put the problem on the board before the bell finished ringing: two countries, two goods, one question. "Explain why both of them gain from trading," he said, "even if one country is better at making both. Presentations Friday. No reading off slides."

William copied the numbers into his notebook. Alpha could make twelve shirts or six computers in a day; Beta could make four shirts or four computers. He understood the arithmetic by Tuesday, could compute the opportunity costs, could see that Beta gave up less to make a computer and should therefore specialize in computers. But when his lab partner Dana asked him at lunch why anyone would trade when Alpha was simply better at everything, he opened his mouth and nothing came out. He had the rule without the reason, which felt like owning a key to a house he'd never seen.

"You're doing the face," Dana said, spearing a fry. "The face you do before you decide something's stupid."

"It's not stupid. I just can't say it in a sentence."

"Then say it in two."

He couldn't. That was the problem, and it had a deadline.

Thursday night his mother dropped him at his grandfather's apartment so she could take the car to her shift, and William spread his notes on the kitchen table while his grandfather made tea. He'd hoped for quiet. What he got was the news playing low, and his grandfather standing at the counter saying, "They finally did it, huh. Raised the rates. About time somebody took inflation seriously." He said it the way he said most things, flat, final, a verdict already rendered.

"Is that good?" William asked, mostly to be talking.

"Good? Inflation's a thief. You save thirty years and it melts your savings. They jacked the rates up like this once before, early eighties, and it broke inflation's back. Best thing that ever happened to the dollar."

William nodded and looked back at his numbers. Then his grandfather sat down across from him, slower than he used to, and turned his mug a quarter turn without drinking.

"I was on second shift at the plant then," he said. "They let go of sixty of us in one afternoon. Unemployment went over ten percent that year. Ten percent. Whole parking lot empty by Friday."

William put his pencil down. His grandfather was not a man who told stories for effect; he told them the way a carpenter sets a nail, once, squarely. The tea steamed between them. On the news, a man in a suit was still praising the rate hikes, and William heard both voices at once, the man on the television and the man at the table, and could not make them into one true thing.

"So it worked," William said carefully, "and it also cost jobs."

"It worked," his grandfather said. "And it cost jobs. Both of those are true, and don't let anybody tell you different."

William drove the idea home in the passenger seat, his mother's headlights carving the dark. He had been trying to parametrize the whole problem as one line, one equation where you solved for the answer. But the numbers on his page were like his grandfather's decade: Alpha gains, Beta gains, and inside each country somebody's parking lot goes empty. The shirts-and-computers version let you total the gains honestly, because the gains were real, both countries could end up with more of both goods than before. What the totals hid was distribution, and hiding it was not the same as lying about it, but it wasn't nothing, either.

Friday he stood up with one index card, on which he'd written nothing. He walked the class through Alpha and Beta, let Dana object that Alpha was better at everything, and then said, "Right, that's the whole point. Better at everything isn't the question. The question is better at what compared to what else you could be doing. Beta's worse at both, but it's less worse at computers. So Beta makes computers, Alpha makes shirts, they trade, and both end up ahead." He saw it land, a small rippling of heads, and felt a flash of exhilaration he tried not to show. Then, before sitting down, he added the part he'd decided he couldn't leave out. "Ahead in total. My grandfather lost his job in the early eighties when they raised rates to kill inflation, and unemployment went above ten percent, and the inflation died anyway. Both happened. I don't know how you weigh that. I'm not sure anybody does."

Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard. "That's not on the test," he said. "But it's germane."

"Is it right, though?" Dana asked as they packed up.

William zipped his bag. "It's honest."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
The protocol sheet had been taped to the inside of the equipment shed since September, curled at one corner, and Brooke had walked past it a hundred times without reading it. She read it now, while the rest of the team did their warmup laps around the far field. After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play. Each step was listed in a column, and beside the column a line said an athlete moved to the next step only while free of symptoms. That was all. It looked almost too simple to matter, like instructions for assembling a shelf.

Priya jogged over from the track, hair still damp from the shower she'd taken after her morning session with the trainer. She had been symptom-free for four days, which was why today was supposed to be light drills, ball work, no contact, no heading. Brooke folded the sheet into her pocket without deciding to.

"You look perspicacious," Priya said, squinting at her. "Or constipated."

"I look like a captain who's down a center back before semifinals." Brooke tossed her the ball. "Ten touches, easy passes, nothing fancy."

The drill was simple by design. Brooke stood twelve yards off and rolled the ball to Priya's feet, and Priya turned and slotted it into an open goal, again and again, the net shivering each time with a small dry sound. The October light came in low across the park, gilding the seed heads in the unmowed strip beyond the touchline. A man flew a kite near the fountain, reeling it in slowly when it dipped.

At the ninth pass Priya stopped. She stood with her hand flat against her forehead, the way people do when a sound has been too loud, and Brooke knew before Priya said anything. "It's back," Priya said. "The headache. It's mild, but it's the same one."

Brooke's first instinct, the one she was least proud of, was to ask whether it was really the same one, or just ordinary tiredness, the kind everyone played through. The second instinct came from the folded paper in her pocket. She took it out and unfolded it against her thigh. The steps ran from rest at the bottom to full play at the top, and Priya was on one of the low ones, light drills, and the rule was that you moved up only while you stayed free of symptoms. There was nothing in the fine print about mild, or about semifinals, or about how badly Fernbrook needed a center back who could read a through ball before it was played.

"You go back a step," Brooke said.

"I know. I hate that I know, but I know."

Coach Renner appeared at the edge of the drill area with his clipboard and his particular talent for arriving at the wrong moment. "How's she looking?" he asked, and Brooke understood that he was asking a different question than the words carried. He had been trying to resuscitate this season since August, when three starters moved away and the league realigned and Fernbrook started drawing schools twice its size. He was not a cruel man. He was a tired one, and Priya's return would have meant something to him beyond the back line.

"Mild headache came back during the drills," Brooke said. "So she steps back a stage. Rest again, or whatever the stage below this is. Then she works up from there."

"We could try her Thursday, see if it clears."

"She stays free of symptoms before she moves up. That's how it works. Every step." Brooke heard her own voice, steadier than she felt. She had wanted Priya on the field so badly that she had almost been willing to translate a headache into something smaller, and the wanting was still there, honest and unresolved, sitting in her chest alongside the decision. Both things were true. She could hold them at once.

Renner looked at the goal, at the kite climbing again near the fountain, at his clipboard. "All right," he said. "Same drill, Priya, you're on distribution with me. No heading."

Priya walked off with him, slower than usual, one hand still at her temple now and then, like someone checking a bruise. Brooke stayed by the goal and re-read the sheet one more time, top to bottom, rest to full play, the small ordered stairs of it. Then she folded it and put it back in her pocket, and called for the next group to bring the balls in.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
story:
Daniel had taped the poster of the mitochondrion to the fence between the lilac bush and the compost bin, and by noon the sun had bleached it to the color of weak tea. He sat on the patio steps with a biology textbook open on his knees, drawing arrows in chalk on the concrete. Glucose went in at the top of the driveway, broke into two smaller pieces near the grill, and the arrows converged at a lopsided oval he had chalked beside the birdbath. Inside the oval he wrote "ATP" and then crossed it out and wrote "makes ATP here," because the poster said the mitochondrion was where most of it got made and he wanted to be able to say why without looking.

The placement exam was in eleven days. If he scored well enough, the college would let him skip introductory biology and go straight into genetics, which was the whole reason he had chosen the school, and also the reason he could not afford to be lazy about the parts he found dull. His sister Maya was home for the weekend, and she came out barefoot with two glasses of lemonade and the particular gravitas of a person who had survived her first year of college and intended for you to know it.

"Quiz me," Daniel said, before she had sat down.

"Fine. Follow one glucose all the way through. Out loud, and if you say 'and then stuff happens,' I'm going inside."

He started at the top of the driveway and walked the chalk path as he talked, crouching to tap each arrow. Glucose split, a small payoff of ATP, some electron carriers loaded, then the oval by the birdbath where the carriers dumped their cargo and the big harvest came out. He could feel the sequence assembling itself correctly for the first time, the way a phrase finally sits right in your mouth after weeks of stumbling.

"You missed where the oxygen fits in," Maya said, but not unkindly. She was peevish about being interrupted from her book and trying not to show it, and the effort made her gentle.

"At the end. It takes the electrons so the whole thing doesn't back up." He took the lemonade anyway. "I actually know that one."

She flipped to the back of his textbook, where he had dog-eared a page with a chart he had been avoiding. "Then what's this? You've bent the corner on the codon table for three days."

"That's not going to be on it. It's genetics, not respiration."

"Read it to me."

He made a face but read it, and somewhere in the middle of the grid of letters he stopped. Every entry was three letters long. There were sixty-four of them. Then he counted the names in the right-hand column, running his finger down the rows, and found only twenty different amino acids. Leucine alone claimed six of the three-letter groups. He counted again with the lemonade glass sweating against his wrist.

"Sixty-four codons," he said slowly. "Three bases each. But only twenty amino acids. So most amino acids have more than one codon." He looked up. "Why would it be built like that? That's, like, redundancy. Like the cell braced itself."

"Beats me," Maya said. "I switched out of bio second semester. But you look like somebody just handed you a prize."

He laughed, embarrassed, and drew sixty-four short chalk ticks in a band along the edge of the patio, then grouped them into twenty clusters, some crowded and some standing alone. It was not respiration. It was not on the exam. But the two systems suddenly felt like they belonged to the same world, one burning fuel to keep the other reading instructions, and he could not make himself regret the detour. Whether the redundancy was sloppiness or protection, or something he did not yet have the words for, he could not say, and he wrote a question mark at the end of the chalk band and left it there.

Maya stood and brushed chalk dust off her shorts. "You know you're going to sit out here until dark."

"Probably," Daniel said. He walked back to the top of the driveway, stood over the chalked glucose with his hands in his pockets, and started again from the beginning.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: A Danish study published in 2019 followed more than 650,000 children and found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism, even among children with autistic siblings.
story:
Seth had the smaller of the two study rooms reserved until five, and his cousin Dez was already fifteen minutes late. He spread the printouts across the table anyway: an article from a parenting blog his aunt had forwarded him, with a highlighted paragraph about a study of twelve children whose parents claimed they changed after the MMR shot, and beside it the library database open on his laptop, where he had been typing search terms for an hour.

Dez came in with a soda he wasn't supposed to have in the room and dropped into the chair across from Seth. "Mom wants me to tell you she's not being irrational," Dez said. "She read things. She sent you the things."

"You're getting the shot Tuesday," Seth said. "For college. So I'm going to figure out what she read." He turned the laptop so Dez could see the screen. The article had a photo of a toddler and a caption in bold type, and the word "cover-up" appeared three times in the first two paragraphs.

"She says twelve kids is twelve real kids," Dez said. "Not a statistic."

Seth scrolled through his database results. He had learned the interface in an hour: filters for peer reviewed, for date, for study type. Most of what came up was small, mouse studies or surveys, until he landed on a Danish study from 2019. He read the abstract twice, then the numbers at the top of the methods section, because he almost didn't believe the first pass.

"This one followed more than 650,000 children," Seth said. "Published in 2019. Danish. No link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Not even in kids who had autistic siblings, which would be the highest-risk group you could pick."

Dez leaned over the table. "Six hundred fifty thousand?"

"More than that. Twelve kids versus more than 650,000." Seth wrote the comparison on the whiteboard in the corner of the room, the way his physics teacher did when two quantities belonged side by side. Twelve on the left, 650,000 on the right. He underlined nothing. The numbers looked different next to each other than they had apart.

"That's a lot of kids," Dez said. "But how do you know they didn't mess it up? The twelve-kid guy could be the honest one."

"That's the thing, I don't know that from one study either way." Seth pulled up the citations. There were other papers citing the Danish one, groups who had run their own numbers in other countries, some of them large, some small, and a letter to the editor that raised a complaint about a variable and a reply that addressed it point by point. He read part of the reply out loud, the dry back-and-forth of two research groups arguing over a definition. "Nobody's saying trust this one paper. They keep checking each other. The twelve-kid thing didn't hold up when other people tried it."

Dez drank his soda. "So it's like, whoever checks the most wins?"

"Sort of," Seth said, then stopped, because that wasn't quite honest. "More like, one result can be a fluke or a lie or bad luck, and you can't always tell which from the outside. But when it's been tried over and over by people who get nothing out of agreeing, that's the closest thing we've got." He looked at the blog article again, at the scathing tone of its last section, where the author called pediatricians whores for pharmaceutical companies and promised that the truth was being cauterized out of the public record. Seth didn't know what the author thought cauterize meant, but the word had a violence to it that made him sit back.

"Are you going to tell Mom she's wrong?" Dez asked.

"I'm going to send her both. The twelve-kid thing and this one, with the numbers. And a note that says one guy with twelve kids isn't the same as a country with 650,000, and that if she still wants to wait, that's her call, but she should see the size of what she's weighing it against." Seth closed the laptop halfway. "I can't make her read it."

Dez stood, crumpled the can, and shot it at the recycling bin by the door. It bounced off the rim and rolled under the microfiche cabinet. "Your sagacity is going to go over great," he said, fishing it out.

"Tuesday," Seth said. "You're still getting the shot."

"Tuesday," Dez said, and held the door open with his foot while Seth gathered the printouts and left the whiteboard as it was, twelve on one side and 650,000 on the other, for whoever had the room next.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
story:
Rosalie had drawn the upstairs hallway four times since dinner, and four times it lay on the page like something flattened under glass. She was sixteen and the portfolio deadline for the summer art intensive was in nine days, and the hallway was supposed to be her proof that she could handle interior space. Instead it looked like a child's diagram of a hallway, doors standing straight up beside each other like cards taped to a wall. She sharpened her pencil until the sharpener drawer was full of gray dust, and then she put her forehead on the desk, which enervated rather than rested her, because from that angle she could see the actual hallway stretching away from her, getting smaller, and her drawing refusing to do the same.

Her little brother Theo was at the kitchen table with his Spanish homework, saying the same word over and over in different wrong ways. "Is it hoop-oh-eh," he asked her when she came down for water, "or hoo-eh? The workbook has this whole section on phonetics and it just makes everything more confusing." She told him it was the second one, though she was only mostly sure, and he wrote it down anyway, trusting her more than the book. Their mother was on the late shift, so the house had that evening quality of everyone solving their own problem in a separate room.

Back upstairs, Rosalie taped the fourth drawing to the wall beside her window and looked at it from across the room. The problem wasn't her line quality. The doors were well observed, the light switch was even in the right place. But nothing receded. Every part of the hallway insisted equally on its own importance, like a paragraph where every sentence was bolded. She thought about asking her mother when she got home, but her mother had gone to art school for two years before dropping out to have her and had an equivocal relationship with all of it, half proud and half sorry, and Rosalie didn't want to walk into that tonight.

So she went to the shelf instead, to her mother's old orange textbook with the cracked spine, the one she wasn't supposed to bend back because the glue was going. It fell open near the middle, as books do, to a page about the Renaissance. She read it standing up, one finger holding the page. Around 1420 in Florence, an architect named Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective. She said the words to herself. Linear perspective. The technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface. She read the sentence twice more, and something in her chest shifted the way a lock shifts.

She sat down fast, before the feeling could leak away, and took a fresh sheet. First she drew a single point in the middle of the paper, low, about where the far end of the hallway would be. Then she drew lines out from it toward the corners and edges of the page. It looked like nothing, like a strange kite, like a drawing of rays. But when she hung the hallway's edges along those lines, the doors slanting inward, the ceiling sloping down toward the point, the whole thing opened. The paper suddenly had a far away in it. She actually laughed, alone, a short surprised sound, and Theo called up through the floor, "Was that you?"

She called him up anyway. He stood in her doorway with his workbook still in his hand, and she turned the paper toward him. "What do you see?"

"A hallway," he said. "It goes back." He leaned in. "What'd you change?"

"Look," she said, and drew a fifth sheet in front of him, point first, then lines, then walls, faster now because her hand knew where it was going. "It's called linear perspective. Lines that meet at a vanishing point." She tapped the dot with her pencil. "Some guy in Florence figured it out around 1420. Brunelleschi. He was an architect."

Theo frowned at the page. "So the floor and the ceiling both go to the same point?"

"They do," she said, and turned the pencil around and shaded the floor lightly, so the hallway had weight as well as distance. She wasn't sure yet whether she could do this with the staircase, or with the kitchen where the window light came from two directions. The book had gone on to other things and she hadn't read them. But the fifth drawing was on the desk getting better, and the portfolio had nine days, and downstairs her mother's car had just pulled into the driveway.

Rosalie carried the drawing down the stairs herself, holding it flat against her chest so it wouldn't bend, and set it on the kitchen table under the light.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
Riley had signed up for the library's Tuesday makerspace because his mother said he needed something that wasn't a screen, and he had stayed because of the kiln, a squat beige cylinder in the corner of the room that smelled like warm chalk. For three weeks he had been building a bowl out of reddish clay his grandmother had left in her garage, wrapped in a plastic bag gone brittle with age. She had taught middle school art for thirty-one years and had died in March, and the clay was, as his uncle put it at the funeral, part of the patrimony, said with a smirk that Riley had decided to ignore. The bowl was for his mother, and her birthday was Friday.

"Last firing before the holiday is at four today," Ms. Ade said, though she mostly ran the 3D printers and left the kiln to whoever was using it. Riley had the whole fact sheet she'd printed from a pottery supplier taped inside his notebook, and he had read it enough times that the numbers felt like a song lyric. Earthenware, which was what his clay was, fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius. Porcelain fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius. He hadn't thought much about the gap between those two sentences until Priya sat down across from him with six pale white cups.

"Are those for Mr. Okafor's class?" he asked. She nodded without looking up, trimming the foot of a cup with a loop tool, her mouth set in the melancholic line of someone working close to a deadline. Her final portfolio was due Monday. His mother's birthday was Friday. The kiln held one load. It was ten past two.

"They can't go in together," Priya said, and he understood at once, though he made her say it anyway, because saying it made it real. "Your clay and mine fire at different temperatures. Yours is earthenware, mine's porcelain. If we put them in the same load, one of us gets ruined." She said it flatly, without drama, and then went back to trimming, which he recognized as a way of not asking him to be the one who yields.

He wanted to argue that his project mattered more, that a birthday was not the kind of deadline you could move, that hers was for a grade and grades could be renegotiated. But even as he assembled the argument he could hear how it would sound, and more than that, he could see the flaw in it, because Priya's cups were six and careful and she had been coming here since September while he had wandered in three weeks ago carrying a bag of dead clay and grief. Still, he didn't want to just give in, either, because surrendering wouldn't be generosity; it would be buying the feeling of being good, and he suspected his grandmother, who had once made a student repaint an entire mural for cutting a corner, would see through it.

So he tried to operationalize fairness instead of just feeling it. Two firings were impossible; Ms. Ade had confirmed that with the schedule pulled up on her tablet. He asked Priya what would happen if her porcelain fired low, below its range, and she said it wouldn't vitrify, wouldn't be what it was supposed to be, and the way she said "supposed to be" told him it wasn't only a technical matter. Then he looked at the fact sheet again, at his own sentence, earthenware fired below about 1,200, and the word "below" opened a small door. His clay could take a lower firing. Her porcelain needed the heat.

"Fire yours high enough for the porcelain," he said slowly, "and mine might not survive. But fire low, within my range, and yours never becomes porcelain. So the load isn't really shared. One of us is borrowing the whole kiln." Priya set down her loop tool and looked at him for the first time. "That's actually the clearest anyone's put it all semester," she said. He felt a flare of pride he immediately distrusted.

They decided by weight of need, which they agreed on with the awkward formality of two people inventing a treaty: her portfolio was Monday, the birthday was Friday, and Ms. Ade, checking her calendar one more time, found a cancellation on Thursday afternoon, a single slot, barely enough time to cool before Friday evening. Riley could fire then. Priya got today. He watched her load the cups through the little peephole of flame, and he carried his bowl home unglazed and unfired, wrapped again in his grandmother's brittle bag, and on Thursday he came back an hour early and sat with the bowl on his lap, tracing the ridges his thumbs had left in the rim.

At 3:50, Ms. Ade put her head around the kiln room door. "Furnace maintenance," she said. "They bumped us. Today's load is the last one until the new year." Riley looked at the bowl, then at Priya's six cups, already glossy and cool on the shelf, finished, done, safe. Then he stood up and started wrapping his grandmother's bag around the bowl again, tucking the corners under like she used to tuck him in.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In the far North Atlantic, the water cools and becomes dense enough to sink, then flows south deep underwater as part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
story:
Isabelle spread the printouts across her grandmother's kitchen table, pushing the sugar bowl and the crossword folded to Thursday aside to make room. The assignment was due Monday: explain to the class, in plain language, how greenhouse gases trap heat, and then walk them through the graph of carbon dioxide measurements across the last century. She had the mechanism half-gestured out already, molecules absorbing the infrared the warm earth radiates and sending it back down, a blanket that thickens as the concentration climbs. The graph was the trouble. The line rose slowly, then sharply, like something waking up, and she could read the numbers but not the meaning behind their shape.

"Grandma, can I practice on you?" she asked. "You're the exact audience, someone who doesn't care about science but has to sit through my talk."

Her grandmother lowered her glasses and pulled her chair over. "I care about you, which is close enough. Go on."

Isabelle started with the sun, the light that passes through the air and warms the ground, the invisible heat that rises afterward and gets caught on its way out. She kept it slow, sketching arrows on the back of an envelope. Her grandfather was at the far end of the table with his coffee, silent as he had been all afternoon, reading nothing, watching the window. He had always been laconic, and since his stroke his few words came slowly and he rationed them, so his silence was hard to read. She used to think it meant he had stopped following along.

"You're doing fine," her grandmother said when Isabelle faltered over the word "infrared." "Slower, though. You talk like you're being timed."

The graph came next. "So this axis is years," Isabelle said, turning the page around, "and this axis is the amount of carbon dioxide, in parts per million. Every year, scientists take the air and measure it, and each point on this line is one of those measurements. The line goes up, and in the last decades it goes up faster." She traced it with her finger, the long shallow climb, then the bend, then the steep run to the top of the page. "The provenance matters, that's what my teacher keeps saying. Where the numbers come from. These aren't guesses. Somebody collected that air, every time."

Her grandmother nodded, then frowned at the steep part. "And what happens to all that gas? Does it just stay over the countries that made it?"

"No, it mixes through the whole atmosphere, that's the thing, it's everyone's." Isabelle hesitated. She had a fact for the ocean, too, something the textbook mentioned in one sentence and moved on from, and she had saved it because it seemed like good news, a secret. "The ocean takes up a lot of the heat. And there's this current, in the far North Atlantic, where the water cools and gets dense enough to sink, and then it flows south deep underwater. It's part of a big system." She reached for the map her teacher had printed, ran her finger from the Caribbean up past Iceland, then down again three thousand meters below the surface. "I thought it was like the ocean cleaning up after us. Sinking the heat where we can't see it."

Her grandfather's cup stopped halfway to his mouth. He set it down and pulled the map toward himself with a slow hand, and Isabelle braced for him to tell her she had it wrong. Instead he tapped the place north of Iceland, twice.

"Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation," he said.

"That's it. That's the name." She wrote it in the margin. "Am I saying it right, the overturning part?"

He nodded, and after a moment he tapped the steep section of her carbon dioxide graph, then the map, then the graph again, and pointed at her. She looked between them for a long moment, the rising line and the deep blue arrow, and understood that he was not confirming her tidy story of an ocean that forgives. He was showing her that the graph and the current were the same project, the same record, measurements threaded together by people over decades. The sinking water was not a clean-up crew. It was one process inside the same warming world, and she did not actually know what happened to it next.

"I had it wrong," she said. "In my head, I made the ocean into a solution. It was nicer that way." Her grandmother reached over and straightened the pages so the graph and the map sat side by side. "So Monday, I'll say what's certain: the gases trap heat, the carbon dioxide line is real and it's climbing, and the ocean's circulation is part of the picture. Then I'll say what nobody knows yet, how much the current might change, and that people are still measuring it. My teacher said the honest part is the hard part." She paused. "Last week I thought the whole assignment was about sounding confident."

Her grandfather slid the pen back to her across the table, his hand steadier than usual, and tapped the empty back of the envelope where her arrows were.

"Draw it," he said. "For them."

She drew the sun, the ground, the heat rising, the gases catching it, and beneath the ocean waves, in careful blue, a current diving deep and turning south.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
story:
Jordan liked to tell people he was basically a scientist already, which was true in the sense that he owned a lab notebook and had once kept a sourdough starter alive for eleven days. He had come to his grandmother's house for the weekend with a chemistry test folded in his back pocket, and by Saturday afternoon he was sprawled on the sunporch floor with the textbook open to a chapter titled "Earth's Energy Budget," narrating his brilliance to anyone within earshot.

"Question one," he announced. "Why does the atmosphere trap heat? And the answer is obvious. Nitrogen and oxygen. They're, like, basically the whole atmosphere, so they must be doing the trapping. More gas, more heat. Done. Next question."

His cousin Priya was at the wobbly card table doing a puzzle of the Eiffel Tower, a thousand pieces of gray that she claimed was relaxing. She did not look up. "You just made that up."

"I deduced it."

"You deduced that the most common gases must be the greenhouse gases. That's not deduction, that's vibes." She reached across the table without moving her eyes off the board, found the textbook's index, and ran her finger down the page. Jordan watched her with the particular dread of a person whose confident claim is about to be fact-checked by a relative. "Here. Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation."

Jordan sat up. "That can't be right. Ninety-nine percent of the air does nothing? Then what's doing all the work?"

"The other one percent, obviously. The benchwarmers." Priya finally looked at him, pleased. "The scrubs are carrying the whole team."

"That's backwards. That's like saying the most popular kids in school have no personality and the weird ones run everything." He pulled the book toward him and read the sentence himself, twice, mouth moving slightly, because he did not fully trust Priya either; she had once convinced him for an entire car ride that our grandmother had been a competitive swimmer, which was chicanery of a high order given that the woman took baths in six inches of water and called it ambitious. But the sentence held. Molecules made of two identical atoms. Both nitrogen atoms the same, both oxygen atoms the same, and apparently sameness made them invisible to infrared, the way you stop hearing a sound that never changes.

The graph on the next page zigzagged upward across a century, and Jordan traced it with his finger, feeling something visceral and inconvenient in his stomach, a small elevator-drop. He had assumed the line would be a smooth hill. Instead it undulated, wobbled, dipped and climbed, as if the atmosphere were a person deciding over and over whether to commit, then committing anyway, higher every decade. He put his finger at the left edge and walked it to the right like a tiny tired hiker.
