"So wait," he said. "My whole answer was backwards, and I was confident about it. I was confident the way Uncle Ray is confident about his fantasy football team."

"Uncle Ray's team is bad," Priya agreed.

"Uncle Ray's team is historically bad." Jordan flipped back and forth between the pages, building the answer again from the floor up: not the giants of the air but the trace players, the carbon dioxide that showed up in the graph like a guest who arrives quietly and rearranges all the furniture. He wrote it out in his notebook, then crossed out his first draft and wrote a second, and then, because honesty seemed suddenly important, a third that began "The most abundant gases are not the important ones here," which felt like a sentence a person could build a life on, or at least a Tuesday.

Their grandmother drifted through with iced tea and offered the opinion that the weather had been strange lately, stranger than when she was young, and that in her day June had known what it was doing. Jordan started to explain about identical atoms and then stopped, because she had already moved on to complaining about a cardinal that kept attacking the kitchen window, a bird she believed was engaged in a personal feud with her. He thought about telling her the cardinal was fighting its own reflection, and decided some confident corrections were better kept to yourself, especially ones you'd been wrong about ninety seconds ago.

He copied the graph into his notebook, redrawing the wobble as faithfully as he could, and labeled the axes, and sat back. There was a version of the story where the air was simple and the biggest things mattered most, and there was this version, where the whole climate turned on actors too minor to notice, and he could not decide which one he liked less.

"One percent," he said to Priya. "The entire planet is being run by the one percent."

She held up a puzzle piece of featureless gray sky. "Somebody has to."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
story:
The party had spilled from the Kowalskis' kitchen onto the lawn, and someone had propped the screen door open with a brick so the music could follow everyone outside. Mathis stood near the folding table with the sheet cake, his mortarboard under one arm, and listened to the tinny march coming from a phone propped against a pitcher of lemonade. It was the same processional they had walked to that afternoon, slowed and flattened by the little speaker, and his cousin Theo was conducting it with a breadstick.

"Best part of the whole day," Theo said. "The walking-in song. Very dignified. Very British."

"Pomp and Circumstance," said Priya, from the class below Mathis's, still holding her plate. "I looked it up once because my mother plays it every June and cries. It's by Elgar."

Mathis had assumed the title meant nothing more than ceremony, that "pomp and circumstance" was simply a fancy phrase for trumpets and gowns. He was about to say so when Dana came around the corner of the house with her cup and stopped, head tilted, the way she did in English seminar when a line of Shakespeare rang a bell somewhere behind her eyes.

"Wait," Dana said. "We studied that. It's Othello. The phrase comes from the play. Othello says it, right at the end, when he's giving up everything: the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war. Elgar took his title from that." She recited it again, quietly, as if testing the weight of it. "Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."

Theo lowered the breadstick. "So our walking-in song is about war?"

"About losing it, sort of," Dana said. "Othello's farewell speech. He's undoing his whole life in it."

The march kept playing, bright and patient, while the cake sweated in the heat. Mathis felt the odd double exposure of it: the tune that had made his grandmother dab her eyes in the gymnasium, and underneath it a general stripping off his sword and his history. He wanted to say something clever, to preempt Theo's next joke, but instead he found himself holding both ideas at once and not being able to drop either one.

The summer before, Mrs. Andaya had taught them the word synecdoche, the part standing for the whole, and had made them find examples all semester until it became a private habit. Now he watched the gowns on the lawn, the sash of a girl dancing badly by the fence, the stolen faculty hood Mr. Brandt had worn backwards, and thought that the costume was the same trick: one garment carrying four years. Elgar had done it with a phrase. He lifted a piece of Othello's ruin and made it stand for beginnings, and now every June, ten thousand gymnasiums played a broken soldier's farewell while parents wept for reasons they would have called happy.

"That's depressing," Theo decided. "I'm going to eat more cake."

"It's not depressing," Priya said. "It's beautiful. It means the ceremony knows something."

Mathis's father was across the lawn talking to Mr. Kowalski about the scholarship fund, the one that paid the deposit for students whose families couldn't, the fund that kept the school from quietly losing its indigent kids between June and September. His father had put money in it every year since Mathis started, quietly, the check written in the kitchen with the same pen used for grocery lists. Mathis had never asked why. Tomorrow his own deposit was due, and his father had already told him not to worry about it.

He crossed the lawn to Dana, who was watching Theo and Priya argue about whether the song could be reclaimed for hope or whether it would always carry Othello underneath, the way a river carries what was dumped upstream.

"Here's what I can't decide," Mathis said. "Whether Elgar was being ironic or whether he meant it straight. Whether it's a joke on all of us, or whether he thought graduating was a kind of glorious war and the phrase fits."

"Maybe he didn't decide either," Dana said. "Maybe that's why it lasts."

The phone by the lemonade looped the march again, and someone turned it up. Theo resumed conducting, grander now, and Priya saluted him with her fork. Mathis put on his mortarboard, crooked, the way it had sat all afternoon, and walked over to the folding table for a second piece of cake.

"Save me the corner piece," Dana called after him. "The one with the most frosting. Consider it my graduation gift."

"That's my piece," Mathis said, and cut it anyway.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
The mock election ballot had been sitting in Claire's binder for three days, folded once, then folded again, until the creases wore the paper thin. Her eighteenth birthday had fallen on a Tuesday in October, and the county's special election on the school levy was exactly six days later, which meant that for the first time in her life the county clerk's record of her would change from a name in a file to a name on a roll. Mr. Okafor had announced it to the class almost casually, the way he announced everything, and then assigned them to research voter turnout around the world and present a comparison on Friday.

"Australia," said Priya, from two rows over, on Thursday night in the emptying classroom where a few of them had stayed to finish their posters. "I found this and I keep rereading it because I thought it was a typo. Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and if you don't vote without a valid reason you can be fined."

"Wait, fined?" Claire put her marker down. "For not voting? Like a parking ticket?"

"Like a parking ticket for democracy," Priya said, and laughed, though her poster was entirely serious, bar graphs of turnout climbing after 1925 like a staircase.

Marcus, who had been slouched near the window drawing a skull in the margin of his notes, sat up a little. "That's insane. You can't make people vote. That defeats the whole point. The point is that you get to choose, including choosing nothing." He was repeating something his father said at dinner, Claire suspected, the way he always did, but she had argued with his father's opinions often enough that it hardly mattered whose they were.

"Choosing nothing is still a choice," Priya said. "It's just a choice someone else pays for." She smoothed a piece of tape across her graph. "You don't get fined if you have a valid reason. They're not dragging people to polls in chains."

Claire found herself not taking either side, which was unusual, because she generally took sides the way other people took stairs, quickly and without looking down. Her mother, who had staffed phone banks in every election since Claire could remember, treated voting as a duty so basic it barely needed language, like breathing or yielding at a stop sign. Her brother Theo, twenty-two and recently desensitized by an overload of political ads to the point where he claimed not to believe in any of it, had told her over text that her one vote was a raindrop and the raindrop should stay home. She had never doubted her mother. But she had also never had to think about it, and thinking about it now felt like picking up a familiar object and noticing its weight for the first time.

"Here's what I can't figure out," she said, pulling her folded ballot out of the binder and unfolding it on the desk between them, creases and all. "Marcus is right that forcing a choice seems to contaminate the choice. But Priya's graph is right that everyone's there. And the levy." She tapped the mock ballot. "This one's for a fake election for practice. But next Tuesday there's a real one, and it decides whether the schools get the money, and half the town will stay home because it's a Tuesday in November and it's raining and the ads have made everyone numb. My brother's not voting because he thinks his vote is nothing. Someone in Sydney who thinks the same thing has to show up anyway, or pay."

"Or pay," Marcus repeated, and frowned at his skull. "That's the part that gets me. Money. It's a quagmire, honestly. You fine people into participating and what do you get? People marking a ballot at random just to avoid twenty dollars?"

"We don't know it's twenty dollars," Priya said. "The article doesn't say the amount."

"That's worse," Marcus said. "An incipient police state that won't even tell you the fine." But he was grinning a little now, and Claire saw the shift happen, the way you see weather change over water. "Okay, but. If everyone has to come, then the candidates have to talk to everyone. Not just the people who already agree with them. That's something."

Claire looked down at the mock ballot, at the two names printed there for treasurer of a student government that met during lunch on Wednesdays, and felt the small absurdity of it. She was eighteen. In six days she would stand in the fire station on Route 9 behind a curtain that smelled like pencil shavings, and she still could not say whether freedom meant the right to abstain or the obligation to show up. Probably the answer was in there somewhere between the two, in the part she couldn't yet see. She believed in showing up. She also believed that belief shouldn't be compelled, and she could not make those two beliefs stop arguing, and she suspected she wasn't supposed to.

"So are you voting Tuesday?" Priya asked her, capping the markers, gathering poster tubes. The hallway had gone quiet; the janitor's cart squeaked somewhere far off.

"I don't know about the fine," Claire said, folding the mock ballot back along its worn creases. "But nobody here has to make me." She slid it into her binder, zipped her bag, and turned off the lamp over her desk.

fact: The USDA advises refrigerating cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature is above 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
The kitchen thermometer, the cheap dial kind that had lived beside the stove since before Edouard could remember, read thirty-four degrees Celsius, and the chocolate refused to cooperate. He had the notebook open on the counter, the one with TEMPERING written on the first page in his own careful hand, and above that word a grid of temperatures he had copied from a video: melt to forty-five, cool to twenty-seven, bring back up to thirty-one and a half, hold, hold, hold. The problem was that his kitchen was already hotter than the chocolate was supposed to get at the end. He stirred the bowl over a pan of warm water and watched the surface sheen go dull at the edges, which the video had said meant the crystals were forming wrong, forming fat and soft instead of tight and glossy.

His brother Marcel was home from his first year of university, and Marcel's contribution to the afternoon was a paper bag of leftover noodles from lunch, sitting on the counter in the sun since noon. It was nearly two o'clock. Marcel lay on the floor of the living room with his phone above his face, fanning himself with a pizza flyer.

"Put those in the fridge," Edouard said.

"They're fine. Cold noodles are disgusting anyway, I'll microwave them at dinner."

"That's not how it works." Edouard wiped his hands on the towel and picked up his own phone, because he was the kind of person who checked. The page he found said that the USDA advised refrigerating cooked food within two hours. He read further, because two hours had almost passed and something in him wanted the noodles to be guilty. There was more: within one hour if the air temperature was above thirty-two degrees Celsius, ninety degrees Fahrenheit. He looked at the dial thermometer again. Thirty-four.

"It's over thirty-two in here," he said. "So it's not two hours for your noodles. It's one. And that hour's gone."

Marcel sat up. "You're telling me the heat makes the food go bad faster, so the deadline is shorter, and since it's already past the short deadline, my dinner is dead."

"That's what it says."

"This heat wave has desensitized me to everything," Marcel said, "including food safety and joy." But he got up, took the bag to the fridge, and stood in the open door for a while, letting the cold air wash over him, and Edouard didn't say anything about the electricity because he was doing the same thing with the bowl of chocolate, holding it near the fridge's breath.

The chocolate was for their mother. It was her birthday on Saturday, and she was supposed to arrive Friday night from Lyon, where she had been since spring, teaching a term of seminars that had somehow become two terms and then a summer contract. Edouard had decided in June that he would make her a box of tempered squares, dark with candied orange, milk with hazelnut, each one snapping clean like a promise about order. He had failed four times already. The first batch bloomed white and streaky. The second never set at all and had to be scraped off the parchment like mud. The third he had refrigerated in desperation, and the video's comment section, full of sycophants praising the chef's every syllable, had still been unanimous about that: fridge chocolate sweats, dulls, softens. Cold sets the outside before the inside and ruins the snap. Tempering had to happen at room temperature, in a room cooler than this one.

He went back to the bowl and began the work of the final stage, warming it in short passes over the water, stirring, testing a smear on his inner wrist the way the video showed, watching for the smear to set dull and dry within a minute instead of staying wet and dark. Marcel had drifted back in and was leaning against the fridge, watching him.

"You know you've been talking to yourself," Marcel said. "Like a whole narration. Now we stir. Now we check."

"It helps me keep the steps straight. The guy in the video does it."

"The guy in the video is performing for an algorithm. You're performing for chocolate."

"It's not a performance, it's precision. If the cocoa butter forms the right crystals, the chocolate sets shiny and it snaps when you break it. If it forms the wrong ones, it bends. It's just chemistry." He caught himself starting down a long explanation of crystal forms and stopped, because Marcel's eyes had already gone vague. "Sorry. That was tangential."

"I understood one word in three, but I liked hearing it," Marcel said. "You sound like her when she talks about her seminars. The same voice."

Edouard stirred and did not answer. The smear on his wrist set, dull and dry, faster than it ever had before, and something in his chest went light and careful at the same time. He poured the chocolate into the molds, tapping each one against the counter to release the air bubbles, and set them on the cool tile of the kitchen floor, away from the window, away from the fridge's warm exhaust at the back. He put the fan on them. Then his phone buzzed on the counter.

It was his mother. He read the message twice. Her Friday flight had been cancelled by the airline, the earliest rebooking was Monday, she was sorry, she was so sorry, could they celebrate on Monday instead, she would make it up to them. She had put a heart. Marcel read it over his shoulder and exhaled through his teeth.

The molds were setting anyway, because chocolate does not wait for airlines. In twenty minutes the first one had gone matte and firm at the edges, and Edouard turned it out onto the board, and the squares came loose whole, glossy as lacquer. He took one and snapped it in half, and the sound was exactly the sound from the video, a clean high crack, and the broken face was smooth and dark with no bloom at all. Five batches, and on the day it finally worked, it was three days early.

Marcel ate the other half of the square without asking, standing there with the cracked piece held between two fingers. "So they keep till Monday?" he said. "In this heat?"

Edouard looked at the board of shining squares, and at the dial thermometer, which still read thirty-four, and at the fridge where the noodles now sat, rescued by the one-hour rule, taking up the shelf. He got out the parchment and began wrapping the squares one by one.

"Help me," he said. "We'll put them on the bottom shelf, behind the yogurt, and we'll bring them back to room temperature slowly, before she sees them."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
The funeral home closed at noon, and it was already ten, so Anthony's mother drove faster than she usually did, both hands on the wheel, the interstate unspooling in long gray ribbons toward the town where his grandmother had lived and, six days ago, had not. In the back seat Anthony held the eulogy in his lap, three paragraphs he had rewritten four times, and beside him his little cousin Marisol played a game on a tablet with the sound off, which he was grateful for.

He had not cried yet. That was the problem he kept circling back to, the way his grandmother used to circle a crossword clue before filling it in pencil. On Monday, two days after the phone call, he had gone to school, taken a calculus quiz, and laughed at something Danny said at lunch, a real laugh, loud enough that people turned. Then he had felt like a criminal. His mother had cried at the kitchen table on Sunday, and his aunt had cried at the airport, and Anthony had sat among all that weeping like a stone in a stream, wondering what was wrong with him.

"Say the part about the loquat tree again," Marisol said, not looking up from her screen. "For the eulogy."

"Grandma planted it the year I was born." He read it to her quietly. His voice sounded normal to him, which also felt like evidence against himself.

His mother glanced in the mirror. "You don't have to read it if it's too much, honey. Your uncle can."

"It's not too much." It wasn't, and that was the thing that frightened him. He had assumed grief worked like a staircase, that everyone climbed the same stairs in order, and that his failure to reach the first one meant he was skipping the whole structure, building a house with no foundation. Somewhere in him he believed that if he didn't break down now, he would break down later, worse, at some inconvenient and devastating time, like a delayed bill.

At a red light outside the county line, he took out his phone and searched the thing he'd been afraid to search: is it normal not to cry after a grandparent dies. The first results were junk, but one was an interview with a psychologist, George Bonanno, who had studied bereaved people for years. Anthony read it twice. Bonanno had found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss. He read it a third time, slowly, the way his grandmother read the fine print on sweepstakes entries.

"Put that away, we're almost there," his mother said, but her voice had no urgency in it, so he read one more line and then put the phone face down on his knee.

The fact rearranged something in him, quietly, the way furniture gets moved in a room you know well. All those afternoons in his grandmother's kitchen, she had never once demanded that he feel a particular thing. When his dog died at eleven, she had said some people cry and some people plant something, and he had planted beans, and she had watered them when he forgot. He had thought she was being easygoing. Now he thought maybe she had known something the staircase people didn't, something he could hold alongside his worry instead of instead of it. He was still uncertain. It was possible he was resilient and it was possible he was numb, and he could not yet tell the difference, and maybe the difference was not even his to diagnose. He would find out by living through the next hours, not by deciding in advance what they should look like.

His grandmother had been a nurse for forty years, and she had kept her old diagnostic manuals on the shelf beside the cookbooks. Once, when he was thirteen, she had explained the word etiology to him over boiled eggs: the cause of a thing, the why behind the what. He had loved the word and never had occasion to use it until now. There was no etiology for how a person grieves, he thought, or rather there were too many, one for every person, which amounted to the same thing as none. Marisol leaned her head against his shoulder, and he let it stay there.

The parking lot of the funeral home was half full, his uncle's truck already there, the front doors propped open with a rubber wedge despite the cold. Anthony folded the eulogy into his jacket pocket. Before they got out, he said, mostly to the windshield, "Did you know resilience is common? That there aren't mandatory stages?" His mother turned around fully, and after a moment she said, "No," and then, softer, "That's good to know." He opened the door and the cold came in around his ankles, and across the lot his grandmother's sister was standing under the bare loquat tree they had driven two hours to be near, waving at them with both hands.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
Parker had spent forty minutes on the last paragraph, because the last paragraph was where the hard words thinned out. The article was in Spanish, from a paper in Valdivia, and it concerned a flood, a river, a regional official, and something the dictionary kept translating as "turbid," which made no sense applied to water until he looked it up a second time and found it meant muddy, clouded, stirred full of sediment. The final paragraph was about a farmer who had lost forty sheep. It was the easiest part to read and he had started there, and when Sra. Ibarra called on him he had forty sheep and no idea what the article was actually about.

Their regular teacher was away on sabbatical that term, and Sra. Ibarra, who had come from the university to replace him, did not believe in translation exercises. "You summarize aloud," she said on the first day. "One minute. In Spanish. From memory." Parker had assumed this would be like the vocabulary quizzes he could pass by cramming on the bus. It was not. In the third week he still had not made it through a full article, and the oral summaries counted for most of his grade, and his mother had already paid the deposit for the spring exchange trip that the district's language grant underwrote, the trip everyone said would change how he thought about everything.

He went second that day, after Marisol Vega, who spoke Spanish at home and summarized the article as though reading it from the air. Parker stood, held his printout, and said that a farmer in the south of Chile had lost forty sheep in a flood. He said the river was turbid. He said the farmer's name might be don Pedro, or the name might have meant something else entirely.

Sra. Ibarra folded her hands. "And what happened in the article?"

He looked at the last paragraph, the sheep, the mud. "The flood," he said.

"Where did you start reading?"

"The end. The end was easier."

She nodded once, which was neither approval nor its opposite, and moved on to Deshawn, and Parker sat down with his ears burning and the article still mostly a locked room in front of him.

Marisol watched him from two seats over. She had noticed him at the start of the term, the way he attacked the page from the bottom like a climber who thought the summit was the easy part, and it had puzzled her, because in her house the newspaper came every morning and her father read the first paragraph of everything, sometimes only the first paragraph, and considered himself informed. She had assumed everyone knew this. But watching Parker, she understood that he did not, and that nobody was going to tell him, because Sra. Ibarra believed in finding things out and because the class was arranged in a quiet competition that made admitting confusion expensive. After the bell she caught him at the door, the printout still in his hand.

"You read it backwards," she said.

"I read the easy part first."

"News is written front-loaded," Marisol said. "It's called the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first, and the less important details follow after, so the opening paragraph carries the core story." She tapped the top of his page. "You did the sheep first. The sheep are the least important thing in there. That's why they're at the end."

Parker looked at the first paragraph, which he had avoided for three weeks because it was dense with official titles and numbers and verbs in tenses he had not yet been taught. He sat down at the nearest desk, and Marisol, instead of leaving for lunch, sat across from him, and for twenty minutes they worked through it with her refusing to translate and him refusing to give up. The first paragraph, it turned out, was the whole story: a regional official had announced that the river's flood defenses had failed, that three towns were being evacuated, and that the blame lay with the previous administration's budget. The sheep were a closing detail, a human face stapled to the end.

The following week he summarized an article about a bus strike in Lima in fifty-three seconds, starting from the top, hitting the core of it in the first sentence, and Sra. Ibarra said "mejor," which from her was a standing ovation. Walking out, Parker found the English teacher, Mr. Okonkwo, in the hallway, who had been laid off by the same budget fights the article described and rehired only after the teachers' union threatened to strike in sympathy. Parker told him about the inverted pyramid, feeling like someone passing on a family secret. Mr. Okonkwo smiled and said that was exactly how he taught it in journalism, back when the school still had a newspaper, and then he paused. "Of course, my students always buried the news in their own articles anyway. Last line, every time. They figured the ending was where the important stuff went." He nodded toward the main office, where the principal's weekly bulletin had just been posted, its announcement of next year's program cuts printed in small type at the very bottom. "Apparently the administration figured the same."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered Kmart still had its lines, faded to the color of old bone, and Arianna's father had chosen it because it was empty on Sunday mornings and close enough to walk to if she refused to drive home. She sat in the driver's seat of his Corolla with her hands at ten and two, exactly where the internet had said, and adjusted the mirror for the third time. Mr. Okafor, the instructor her father had hired, settled into the passenger seat with a clipboard and a thermos and the unhurried air of a man who had survived four hundred first lessons.

"Before we touch anything," he said, "a question. You're going twenty kilometers an hour and you brake, and the car stops in, say, one car length. Now you double your speed, you're going forty. How much longer to stop?"

Arianna considered the lines of the lot, the light pole at its far edge, the arithmetic of it. "Twice as long," she said. "Double the speed, double the distance. That seems fair."

"That seems fair," Mr. Okafor repeated, and wrote something on his clipboard. "Keep that answer in your pocket. We'll come back to it."

They began with the pedals, dry, engine off, her foot learning the difference between the brake's firmness and the clutch's vagueness. Then he had her start the car and creep forward in first gear, stall twice, creep again. The lot was enormous and blank, and the emptiness made her bold in a way she hadn't expected; by the fourth circuit she was doing thirty along the back row of the lot, feeling the steering loosen and the car begin to feel less like a machine she was operating and more like something she was wearing.

"Good," Mr. Okafor said. "Now we do the stopping test. See that cone?" He had placed a single orange cone near the middle of the lot sometime before she'd arrived, and she had assumed it was decoration. "Drive toward it at twenty and brake at the line, the painted one, just before it. Then we do it at forty. Same line, same cone."

At twenty she braked at the line and stopped with the cone just beyond her bumper, close enough that she could see the scuff marks on its base. She circled back, aligned herself, and brought the car up to forty, which felt suddenly like real speed, the light pole and the Kmart sign sliding past in her peripheral vision. She braked at the painted line exactly as before. The car sailed past the cone, past the space where the cone's shadow lay, and shuddered to a stop a full four car lengths farther on, close enough to the lot's far curb that Mr. Okafor's hand had risen quietly toward the emergency brake.

"You didn't do it wrong," he said, as she sat gripping the wheel and breathing. "The car did that. Tell me how far you went."

Arianna looked back at the cone, small and patient in the mirror, and counted the painted stalls between it and her rear bumper. One car length at twenty. She counted again, because the number seemed like a trick, some sophistry of perspective or of her own counting. Four. "Four car lengths," she said. "Not two. Four." She heard her own answer from fifteen minutes ago, double the speed, double the distance, and felt the particular embarrassment of having been confidently wrong in front of someone whose opinion she was paying to acquire. At school she had learned to argue both sides of any question and call it rigor, to construct a defense of whatever position was convenient, and she recognized now that she had been applying that same fluency to the physical world, as if the pavement would accept a counterargument.

"Braking distance goes up with the square of your speed," Mr. Okafor said, not lecturing, just confirming, tapping his clipboard. "Twice the speed, about four times the distance to stop. At highway speeds it's the whole reason you leave gaps."

"Four times," she said. "It's not negotiable. There's no version where I'm quick enough for it to be two."

"Not one."

She thought of her mother, who drove with two fingers on the wheel and a lifetime of assumptions about her own reflexes, and of her father, who followed at three car lengths and had been called timid for it. She had believed, without ever saying so, that caution was mostly affective, a mood people chose, something that would atrophy in her if she indulged it too often. But the distance wasn't a mood. It was a law she hadn't known and couldn't charm, and the strange thing was that knowing it didn't make her want to drive less. It made the whole business feel suddenly adult, a contract with consequences she could now measure in painted stalls. What she couldn't yet decide was where the caution should live: in her foot, in the gap ahead of her, or in some habit of mind she hadn't built yet. That part stayed open, and she let it.

"Again," she said, and swung the wheel around, easing back across the empty lot toward the little orange cone.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do.
story:
Madison's mother had a rule about the Saturday shop: whoever rode along got to carry the baskets, and whoever was learning to drive got the car afterward. So Madison stacked tins of beans into the trolley with the grim efficiency of someone earning wages, and her mother hummed along to the radio playing above the dairy aisle, and the whole time Madison was thinking about the letter from the test centre. Her practical driving test was on Thursday, and in the margin of the confirmation email, in her instructor's neat handwriting, was a note that had been bothering her for a week: "We've done bay parking. We should talk about the others."

"There's more than one?" Madison had asked, and Priya had said, brightly, too brightly, "We'll cover it Tuesday," which was the day before the test, which was like being told about a pop quiz the night before it happened.

At the checkout her mother fumbled for her card and Madison loaded the bags, and the boy at the till, maybe nineteen, wearing a lanyard that said TRAINEE MANAGER, asked if she'd found everything all right. She said yes. Then, because the queue behind them was long and nobody was talking, she said, "Do you drive?"

"Passed last year," he said, scanning a bag of spinach with a beep that sounded almost sarcastic. "Failed once first. Parallel parking. I'd only practised in car parks, so when he asked me to do it at the side of the road, I just sort of... stopped."

"At the side of the road?"

"That's where they get you. Bay parking's the safe one, in the car park. Out on the road it's one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner can ask for. Mine picked parallel. My mate got the bay. It's luck of the draw."

Madison stood very still with a bag of potatoes in her hands. Her mother said, "Madison, love," and nudged her forward, but Madison was doing arithmetic. Tuesday. One session. One manoeuvre she had never once attempted, out of a hat she could not see into, on a road where the examiner might simply point at a parked car and say there, please.

In the car park she took the driver's seat while her mother fussed with the receipt. Between the trolley bays, an old Vauxhall sat at the kerb, and Madison studied it the way she imagined an examiner might. Two car lengths of empty road behind it. A delivery van ahead. She put her seatbelt on.

"What are you doing?" her mother asked.

"Practising."

"On what?"

"On that." She nodded at the Vauxhall. "Parallel parking. At the side of the road." She reversed out of their space, looped the car park twice, and drew up alongside the Vauxhall, close enough that her mother made a small sound, not quite a word. Madison checked her mirrors, which she did now the way other people checked their phones, constantly and without thinking. Then she began the reverse, turning the wheel full lock, watching the nearside wing mirror like it owed her money.

She ended up eighteen inches from the kerb and a foot from the Vauxhall, angled slightly. Not perfect. But a car, in a space, at the side of a road.

"Is that it?" her mother asked. "Are we done? Can we go home?"

"One more." She pulled forward and did it again, worse, then a third time, better, and a fourth, when a woman with a trolley stopped to watch with the frank interest of someone at a zoo. Madison wound down the window. "Sorry. Test on Thursday."

"Bay or road?" the woman asked.

"Road, if I'm unlucky."

"Both," the woman said. "Practise both, then luck's got nothing to do with it." She pushed her trolley on toward the Vauxhall, which, Madison now noticed, had a man asleep in the driver's seat, undisturbed by any of it.

Driving home, Madison felt something settle, not into certainty exactly, but into something adjacent to it. Priya's cheerful vagueness had impugned nothing and promised nothing; the trainee manager's confession had given the thing its true shape: not a hidden trap but a known list, one item short in her case. She could not make Thursday's examiner choose the bay. She could only remove the difference between the choices, and she had until Tuesday, and Priya, she suspected, had known she'd figure that out, had counted on a kind of complicity between them, the unspoken agreement that a panicked pupil is worse than an informed one.

The motorway ramp came up on her left, and she signalled early, matched her speed to the flow, and merged into the gap behind a lorry whose driver flashed his lights at her, which she had learned meant well done, come on. Her mother gripped the door handle less than she used to.

"They might not even ask for it," her mother said, as their junction approached. "The parking. You might get the easy one."

"Or I'll reverse around a corner," Madison said. "That's a manoeuvre too, apparently. The internet is a pugnacious place at two in the morning."

At the roundabout she slowed, looked right, and waited. Behind the grocery bags in the boot, something shifted and rolled, one of the tins, probably, finding its level.

"Left at the next one," her mother said. "Then you can practise the hill start on our road, and after that, honestly, you're on your own, because I've done my part and my part was tins."

Madison indicated left.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, which won the 1993 Bancroft Prize, argued US leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world.
story:
Levi had the museum's third-floor gallery almost to himself on the Tuesday before school started, which was the point of coming. His backpack held two books on the French Revolution, a photocopied packet of excerpts, and a half-empty notebook with the words "HOW VIEWS CHANGED SINCE 1800" underlined twice at the top of a blank page. He stood in front of a case holding a cockade, its ribbon faded to the color of rust, and tried to imagine Burke looking at one of these and feeling the world come apart.

The assignment terrified him in a way he had not admitted to anyone. His older sister, Devi, had told him that a historiographical essay was not about what happened but about how historians had argued, and the distinction, which had sounded simple in her kitchen, kept dissolving when he tried to write. He had Burke's reaction, Carlyle's drama, the Marxist reading, the revisionists of the 1980s who said class had been the wrong lens all along. He had the facts. What he lacked was a way to hold them together without flattening them into a timeline with a moral at the end.

He moved along the cases slowly, because the gallery guard, a small woman named Mrs. Okafor whose badge he had read on previous visits, had once told him that slow looking was the whole trick of museums, and he had decided to believe her. "You're back," she said, coming over to straighten a label someone had knocked crooked. "Same bag, same frown."

"College essay," Levi said. "Sort of. It's about how people have seen the French Revolution differently since 1800, and I can't figure out if the historians are arguing about the Revolution or about themselves."

Mrs. Okafor considered the cockade case as if it might answer. "Maybe they're arguing about the present, using the past as the room to do it in." She pointed down the corridor. "There's a display on how museums change their own exhibits. Same idea, smaller scale. And the library room is open if you need to sit."

The library room, it turned out, was less a library than a reading alcove with a shelf of exhibition catalogs and a few donated books of history. Levi sat down anyway, mostly to have somewhere to put his despair, and texted Devi: "I have nine historians and no argument. Every time I line them up they cancel each other out."

Her reply came while he was still staring at a catalog called Revising the Revolution. "Stop trying to make them agree. Pick two who genuinely clash and build the essay on the seam between them. Also: look up what historians do in other fields when the big interpretation breaks. That's your model. It doesn't have to be France."

He almost put the phone down. Then he thought about what she had said, the seam rather than the summary, and began pulling catalogs off the shelf. The Cold War was not his subject, but a fat blue book had a prize sticker on its spine, and he opened it because the sticker said Bancroft, which Devi had once mentioned the way other people mentioned the Pulitzer. The book was Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, and its argument, compressed into the introduction, stopped him cold. Leffler had won the 1993 Bancroft Prize for maintaining that American leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world. Where other historians Levi had heard of, especially someone named Gaddis, saw defense and containment, Leffler saw the pursuit of preponderance itself, security achieved by standing above everyone else.

He read the introduction twice. What gripped him was not the Cold War at all but the shape of the disagreement: two historians, the same archive, opposite readings, and the argument was really about what the country was for. That was his seam. If historians of the Revolution had split the same way, then his essay was not a timeline but a set of running questions: who feared the crowd, who trusted it, and what present danger each historian was answering when he looked back at 1789.

He worked for two hours, filling pages, and at some point Mrs. Okafor brought him a cup of water without being asked, setting it on the far side of the table away from his notebook. "You looked like a man in the desert," she said. He thanked her and noticed that the afternoon light had shifted through the tall windows, and that the museum's diurnal rhythm was closing around him, guards rotating, voices thinning, the front desk cashing out.

By closing time he had a plan and a problem. The plan: pair the Marxist historians with the revisionists and show that the disagreement was about the present, not the past, using the Leffler model as his structuring idea without pretending the Cold War explained France. The problem: he did not actually know whether the Marxist reading was really dead after 1989 or whether the revisionists had overcorrected, and every time he tried to resolve it he circumscribed his own argument until it said nothing. He wrote in the margin of his notebook, "I don't know who is right. I know what each side was afraid of. Is that enough?" and, after a minute, added, "Maybe that's the essay."

He packed slowly. At the door Mrs. Okafor was logging the last visitors out, and she nodded at his bag. "Did you find your seam?"

"Maybe," Levi said. "I found a book about the Cold War instead of the French Revolution, and it told me how to write about the French Revolution. But half my historians still won't line up."

"Good," she said, and held the door for an elderly couple shuffling toward the exit. "The ones who line up too neatly are usually hiding something."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
Ms. Ruiz had a clock on her wall that ticked too loudly for a room where people were supposed to say private things, and Naomi had decided, over four visits, that she hated it. She sat with her hands folded on the folder of printouts, waiting to be told, one more time, what she already knew.

"Your list is all reach schools," Ms. Ruiz said, turning the paper toward her. "Where's the safety?"

"She'll say the state school," Naomi said, meaning her mother, though her mother wasn't in the room. "She calls it the fallback, which is her word for failure."

"That's not what it means to her," Ms. Ruiz said, mild, and Naomi thought, you've met her twice, you don't get to translate her. But she only shrugged, because arguing took energy she was saving for the wait, which had begun to feel like a job in itself. Every morning she checked the portal of the faraway school, the one in the city with the studio art program, and every morning the status read the same two words, and she had trained herself to look away before the words could arrange themselves into a verdict.

The night before, she and her mother had sat at the kitchen computer until nearly one. The state deadline was the next day, and her mother had printed the instructions and read them aloud in her careful, slow way, the way she read anything official, as if the government might be listening for mistakes. The form was called the FAFSA, her mother said, tapping the screen, and it was how you applied for federal financial aid, the Pell Grants and the federal loans. Naomi had assumed the loans were the whole point, that the form was basically a debt application dressed in a cheerful acronym, a bureaucratic dysphemism if she'd ever heard one, though she kept that to herself. Then her mother's finger moved down the page. The states used it too, she read, and the colleges, for their own aid. Their own money, Naomi said slowly, money we haven't even applied for yet, and her mother said, well, that's what it says, and for a while neither of them spoke, just the furnace cycling on in the basement.

"Choleric" was the word Ms. Ruiz had used in October, not about Naomi but about the father in the novel they'd ended up discussing when Naomi came in claiming it was about course registration. She'd meant the character, but Naomi had taken it home and tried it on her mother and found it almost fit, her mother's quick flare over the electric bill, over the guidance office's voicemail, over the word "fallback." Almost fit. This morning her mother had driven her to school early so they could finish the form's last page in the car, phone hotspot on, both of them hunched over the small screen, and when Naomi hit submit her mother had put a hand flat on the dashboard, not a victory gesture, just steadying, and said, "Okay. Okay. Now they know we exist."

The trouble was that Naomi had spent months thinking about college as a problem you could parametrize, like the curves in calculus: set the variables, tuition and distance and prestige, plot the points, find the feasible region. Her mother lived inside a different math entirely, one where you applied everywhere the form reached and let the money tell you where home would be. For a long time Naomi had filed her mother's method under the heading of giving up, and she was honest enough, sitting under the ticking clock, to admit the filing had been wrong, or at least premature, which in her experience was the same thing as wrong but softer to hold.

"So what do you want from me today," Ms. Ruiz asked. "You've submitted everything. There's nothing left to do but wait."

"I want you to tell me the waiting means something," Naomi said. "That checking the portal helps. That it's not just a slot machine."

Ms. Ruiz didn't answer right away, which Naomi disliked and also trusted. Outside, someone's class change filled the hallway with noise, then emptied it.

"My mom wants me to add the state school," Naomi said. "I told her it was a fallback. She got quiet. She does that instead of fighting."

"Is that what it is to you?"

Naomi looked at the folder, at the printouts her mother had made at the library because their printer was out of ink, the pages still warm when she'd slid them across the table. "It's money we could actually get," she said. "It's a place with a real studio. I don't know if that's settling or if I was being proud and calling it standards."

Ms. Ruiz slid a blank add form across the desk and set a pen on top of it. "You don't have to decide what it means today."

Naomi picked up the pen and wrote the state school's name, her letters smaller than usual, careful, and then she looked up and asked, "Can I use your phone? My mom's at work, and she'll want to know before I lose my nerve."

" Dial nine for outside," Ms. Ruiz said, and turned back to her computer as Naomi started pressing the buttons.
